india-lpm.title: Offline-first is a baseline requirement for Kerala's forest-area tribal students, never an optional enhancement

content.label: Offline-first is a baseline requirement for Kerala's forest-area tribal students, never an optional enhancement
content.statement: Any curriculum content built for Kerala's forest-dwelling Scheduled Tribe communities must be designed to be downloaded once (at a school, hostel, or known connectivity point) and used completely without a live connection afterward -- not "mobile-friendly," not "works offline as a fallback," but offline as the default assumption content has to survive. Kerala's existing flagship digital-education delivery (KITE/Samagra/First Bell) is a live-broadcast-plus-streaming model; documented forest hamlets in Wayanad and Attappady show gaps not only in connectivity but, in some specific cases, in electricity itself. A design that assumes "has a phone, just needs better connectivity" will not reach the students most in need of reaching.
content.rationale: Directly grounded in a real, documented gap between Kerala's own digital-education design and the on-the-ground reality in specific named hamlets -- not a generic "rural India has connectivity problems" assumption.

provenance.contributor_notes: First-draft policy principle, not yet reviewed by the planned outside anthropological reviewer or anyone with direct knowledge of these communities.

india-lpm.title: A community's own knowledge must stand on equal footing with state/global curriculum content, never serve merely to illustrate it

content.label: A community's own knowledge must stand on equal footing with state/global curriculum content, never serve merely to illustrate it
content.statement: Where a unit brings in a tribal community's own knowledge (forest ecology, medicinal-plant use, land management, oral history), that knowledge must be presented as genuinely valid on its own terms: a real way of knowing. It must never be treated as decorative material layered onto an unchanged state-curriculum core, and its validity must never depend on confirming a "real" scientific explanation. Science educators working on exactly this problem (Aikenhead's "multi-science" critique of tokenized Indigenous content in STEM curricula; Nakata's "cultural interface" as a space for dialogue rather than a one-way translation) describe this as the central, recurring failure mode of integration efforts that mean well. Even a celebrated bridging framework like "Two-Eyed Seeing" has a real, published critique (Broadhead & Howard, 2021) arguing it can still end up subordinating Indigenous knowledge to Western validation -- this principle names that risk explicitly rather than assuming a bridging metaphor alone solves it.
content.rationale: This is the single most consequential design commitment for "navigating the space between local and global knowledge" as the founding brief for this work describes it -- and the research behind it deliberately includes documented failure modes alongside success stories, per Dustin's own framing of the task.

provenance.contributor_notes: First-draft policy principle, not yet reviewed by the planned outside anthropological reviewer or anyone with direct knowledge of these communities.

india-lpm.title: Build for one specific, named community at a time -- never a generic 'tribal' category

content.label: Build for one specific, named community at a time -- never a generic 'tribal' category
content.statement: Kerala's own real precedents for bridging indigenous and formal schooling are all community-specific. None of them are pan-tribal: KIRTADS' Paniya-language primers are Paniya-specific; the "Padippurasi" bridge workshop was built specifically for Muthuvan children in Edamalakudy; the "Gothrabandhu" mentor-teacher model recruits mentors fluent in the specific local dialect of the school they serve. Paniya, Kattunaikkan, Irula, Muduga, Kurumba, Mannan, Malayarayan, Kurichiya, Cholanaikkan, and Muthuvan are documented as distinct communities with different languages, livelihoods, social structures (e.g. Kurichiya's matrilineal clan system), and circumstances (e.g. Cholanaikkan and Koraga are Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups with populations in the low hundreds; others number in the tens of thousands) -- a model LPM must not flatten this real diversity into one "tribal module," even with good intentions.
content.rationale: Grounded directly in this session's own research, which repeatedly found real, named, non-interchangeable communities rather than one undifferentiated population -- and in the documented critique (found in the same research pass) that generic applications of frameworks like "funds of knowledge" risk homogenizing exactly this kind of real diversity.

provenance.contributor_notes: First-draft policy principle, not yet reviewed by the planned outside anthropological reviewer or anyone with direct knowledge of these communities.

india-lpm.title: Real consultation with a community's own knowledge-holders has to come before building content about that community

content.label: Real consultation with a community's own knowledge-holders has to come before building content about that community
content.statement: Citing a published ethnographic or news description of a community is not the same as that community's own knowledge-holders having been consulted about how their knowledge is represented or used in schooling. Before any unit draws on a specific community's own knowledge beyond what is already publicly documented, this project requires real consultation with that community (ideally through people and institutions already connected to it, such as Oorukoottam hamlet-level councils, Gothrabandhu mentor-teachers, or researchers who already work directly with the community) -- in the spirit of UNESCO LINKS' Free, Prior and Informed Consent principle and Linda Tuhiwai Smith's critique of extractive research that studies indigenous communities without being accountable to them.
content.rationale: This principle exists specifically to name the limits of this founding pass's own research, which was built entirely from published government, news, and academic sources -- real and carefully sourced, but not a substitute for consultation with the communities it describes. Nothing in this repository should be read as having already done that consultation.

provenance.contributor_notes: First-draft policy principle, not yet reviewed by the planned outside anthropological reviewer or anyone with direct knowledge of these communities.

india-lpm.title: Give students and teachers real, jointly-made pathway choices, mapped onto KCF's own standards and governance -- not a parallel track

content.label: Give students and teachers real, jointly-made pathway choices, mapped onto KCF's own standards and governance -- not a parallel track
content.statement: Student agency and teacher-student co-agency need a concrete mechanism. Here is one: for a given KCF-mandated competency, a student and their teacher jointly choose which local/community knowledge strand to pursue in meeting it (e.g. a forest-ecology unit met through a Wayanad student's own community's land knowledge vs. a coastal student's own community's fishing knowledge), and jointly document that choice and its reasoning as part of the assessed work itself -- making the choice-making itself visible and valued alongside the final answer. This is deliberately designed to run through KCF's own existing machinery (its stated critical-pedagogy/social- constructivist foundation, and the Tribal Education Committee governance structure it already mandates) rather than as a competing framework schools would have to adopt instead of KCF.
content.rationale: Answers the founding brief's explicit request for "teacher-student co-agency in developing flexible, valued learning pathways" with a specific mechanism, grounded in what KCF 2023 already commits to (critical pedagogy, social constructivism, a real governance structure for tribal education) rather than inventing a parallel structure that would compete with, rather than work inside, the state curriculum this project needs to stay compliant with.

provenance.contributor_notes: First-draft policy principle, not yet reviewed by the planned outside anthropological reviewer or anyone with direct knowledge of these communities.

india-lpm.title: Kerala's Class 10 Biology retains full evolution/human-origins content NCERT deleted nationally

content.label: Kerala's Class 10 Biology retains full evolution/human-origins content NCERT deleted nationally

objects.subject: Science (Biology)
objects.licenseOrRightsNote: Paraphrased from news coverage of NCERT's own rationalisation exercise, not a reproduction of NCERT's curriculum text or internal notification.

objects.subject: Biology
objects.sourceDocument: SCERT Kerala Class 10 Biology textbook, Chapter 8, 'The Paths Traversed by Life' (pp. 123-137)
objects.licenseOrRightsNote: SCERT Kerala's textbooks carry a bare copyright notice ("© Department of General Education, Government of Kerala") with no stated reuse license anywhere checked (the textbook's own imprint, the KCF 2023 landing page, the Samagra distribution portal) -- unlike Karnataka's CC BY-SA-licensed KOER content, this is described here only at the structural/paraphrase level, not quoted verbatim, pending the same kind of legal review this repo already applies to NCERT/CBSE content.

content.summary: Kerala's Class 10 Biology textbook devotes a full chapter (pp. 123-137) to evolution, covering chemical-origin-of-life theories (Oparin-Haldane, Panspermia, the Urey-Miller experiment), a geological timeline from life's origin through multicellularity, Lamarckism and Darwinism (including the Galapagos finches and Malthus's influence), Neo-Darwinism, and four independent lines of evidence for evolution (fossil, comparative-morphology, biochemical, and molecular -- including a beta-hemoglobin amino-acid-difference comparison table showing chimpanzee at zero differences from humans, gorilla at one, and rat at thirty-one). A dedicated section, "Evolution of Human beings" (p.134), places humans within Anthropoidea and Hominoidea and includes a named hominin-lineage diagram: Ardipithecus ramidus, Australopithecus afarensis, Homo habilis, Homo erectus, Homo neanderthalensis, Homo sapiens, each with a fossil- discovery location. This is the exact category of content NCERT removed from its own national textbooks in the 2023-2024 rationalisation exercise -- Kerala's own chapter was not itself revised in response (it is the pre-existing 2019 edition), but Kerala's state-level decision to keep teaching this content, formalized as a public stance against the national deletion, makes this specific chapter's continued existence a directly relevant data point, not incidental.
content.policyRelevance: A concrete instance of state-level curriculum autonomy (India's constitutional "Concurrent List" status for education, already noted elsewhere in this repo re: Karnataka/Tamil Nadu) being exercised specifically to preserve evolution-education content against a national deletion -- directly relevant to this project's own mission, independent of the separate licensing-rights question this repo otherwise tracks state by state.
content.exhaustivenessCaveat: This repo has not independently read NCERT's own rationalisation notification or its post-deletion textbook text directly this session -- the national side of this comparison rests on news coverage, not a primary NCERT document (see INLP-EVENT-ncert-rationalisation-evolution-deletion's own caveat). No verbatim text from Kerala's textbook is reproduced here, by design -- see each object's own licenseOrRightsNote. The chapter summary above describes real, page-cited structure and topic coverage, not Kerala's own sentences.

provenance.contributor_notes: Kerala's chapter content (title, page range, section structure, topic list, the hemoglobin comparison figures, the named hominin lineage) was read directly from the actual 2019-edition PDF on Kerala's own Samagra portal, both volumes. The national side rests on secondary news coverage, not a primary NCERT document -- see exhaustivenessCaveat.

india-lpm.license_or_rights_note: Paraphrased from news coverage of NCERT's own rationalisation exercise, not a reproduction of NCERT's curriculum text or internal notification.

india-lpm.title: KCF 2023 names Scheduled Tribe children as needing equity support, but its English text names no specific tribal community, language, or place

content.label: KCF 2023 names Scheduled Tribe children as needing equity support, but its English text names no specific tribal community, language, or place

objects.subject: Whole-framework (all subjects)
objects.licenseOrRightsNote: Described from a direct full-text read/search of the official English PDF; no extended verbatim passage reproduced.

content.summary: KCF 2023 explicitly names Scheduled Tribe children among groups needing "special care and support" (alongside Dalits, coastal communities, children of migrant/guest workers, and children with special needs) and mandates a "Tribal Education Committee" as a required sub-section of every local Panchayat Education Committee -- a real governance mechanism, going beyond a sentence of concern. The same document gives mother-tongue medium of instruction deep pedagogical grounding (citing Vygotsky, Chomsky, Gandhi, and Tagore) as essential to cognitive development, and states Kerala follows "a tri-lingual curriculum" with Tamil, Kannada, Arabic, Sanskrit, or Urdu available as a first language alongside Malayalam. However, a direct full-text search of the official English PDF found no mention anywhere of any specific tribal community (e.g. Paniya, Irula, Kattunaikkan, Adiya, Mannan, Cholanaikkan), any tribal language, the districts Wayanad or Attappady in a current tribal-policy context, residential/hostel schooling for tribal children, or a dedicated curricular unit on tribal/indigenous local knowledge. The document's mother-tongue discussion is framed entirely around Kerala's major language communities (the tri-lingual list above); it is never extended to a tribal language. Its one use of the phrase "local knowledge" is a general statement about strengthening the regional economy. It is not a tribal-education-specific goal. The gap, in other words, is not that KCF 2023 is silent on equity -- it names Scheduled Tribes directly and creates a real governance structure for them -- it is that the document's own well-developed pedagogical machinery for mother tongue and local knowledge never cross-references the specific population it separately commits to supporting.
content.policyRelevance: This is exactly the "space between local and global knowledge" this project's own brief asks about, made concrete and checkable rather than asserted in the abstract: the state curriculum has the conceptual tools (mother-tongue pedagogy, local-knowledge framing, a named equity commitment and governance mechanism for tribal students) but has not yet connected them to each other for this specific population, at least not in the document this repo could read. A model LPM for Kerala's diverse communities has a real, specific opening here: connecting machinery the state has already built for other purposes, rather than inventing a parallel structure that competes with KCF.
content.exhaustivenessCaveat: This is a careful absence-of-evidence finding from the English edition of KCF 2023 only. It does not rule out that the Malayalam edition, subject-specific syllabi, or individual textbooks (as opposed to the framework document itself) carry tribal-specific content -- that was explicitly out of scope for what this session could check. It also does not establish what KCF 2007 (the predecessor framework) said, since only KCF 2023 could be full-text-searched this session. This finding should be presented to an outside reviewer as "the framework document's English text does not name these specifics." It should not be presented as "Kerala's curriculum ignores tribal communities" -- those are different claims, and only the first is actually supported here.

provenance.contributor_notes: The "special care" language, the Tribal Education Committee mandate, the mother-tongue pedagogical grounding, and the tri-lingual-curriculum statement were all located via direct full-text search of the downloaded official PDF. This was not based on a secondary description. The negative finding (no named tribal specifics) is the result of the same full-text search returning no matches for a deliberately broad set of search terms (community names, district names, "tribal language," "indigenous," "Adivasi"). It is not an assumption.

india-lpm.license_or_rights_note: Described from a direct full-text read/search of the official English PDF; no extended verbatim passage reproduced.

india-lpm.title: Kerala's flagship digital-education delivery model (First Bell/Samagra) assumes electricity and connectivity that documented tribal forest hamlets do not reliably have

content.label: Kerala's flagship digital-education delivery model (First Bell/Samagra) assumes electricity and connectivity that documented tribal forest hamlets do not reliably have

objects.subject: Educational technology / digital-learning policy
objects.sourceDocument: KITE 'Functions and Duties' page; First Bell programme description

objects.subject: On-the-ground reporting, Wayanad and Attappady tribal hamlets
objects.gradeLevel: Primary and secondary, several specific hamlets
objects.sourceDocument: Onmanorama (1 Sept 2021, Madamkunnu hamlet); The Morning Voice (27 Sept 2026, Attappady power outage); The Caravan (15 Oct 2020)

content.summary: Kerala's own digital-learning infrastructure (KITE, the Samagra portal, and the First Bell programme built on top of them) is fundamentally a live-broadcast-plus-streaming model: content is watched on TV or streamed via app/YouTube. It is not distributed as a downloadable, store-and-forward package designed to work with no connection at all. Kerala's own documented response for students without a TV or internet during COVID-19 was organizational rather than technical: "Neighbourhood Study Centres" with subsidized shared TVs, and a public device-donation drive -- which helps a student without a device but does not help a student whose hamlet has no electricity or signal at all. Independent, directly-read local reporting shows this second case is real and recurring. It is not hypothetical: in September 2021, 31 students in Wayanad's Madamkunnu hamlet had no reliable electricity to charge any device, with some students walking 1.5km to a paid charging point; a September 2026 report (less independently corroborated, flagged separately in this repo's timeline/actor records) describes a 20-day power outage across four Attappady hamlets after storm damage to an underground cable; and a 2020 report on Nilambur/Attappady PVTG communities quotes education officials arguing that reopening residential hostels was the only realistic way to reach children from Kerala's five "primitive" (Particularly Vulnerable) tribal groups. Better streaming alone would not have reached them: they lacked electricity entirely and lived far from any community viewing point. This project's own framing -- students who often have a phone or laptop but no reliable internet -- undersells the severity found in some of these specific documented cases. In the most severe of them, electricity itself is the gap, and connectivity alone does not capture it.
content.policyRelevance: Directly actionable for this project's own design work: an offline-first content model for Kerala's forest-area tribal students cannot assume First Bell/Samagra's existing delivery mechanism is a sufficient base to build on, since that mechanism itself assumes connectivity (and often electricity) the documented cases show is not universal. A genuinely offline-first design needs to plan for content that survives being downloaded once (at a school, hostel, or connectivity point) and used entirely without a connection afterward, and in the most severe documented cases, without reliable power either.
content.exhaustivenessCaveat: This finding draws on a patchwork of separately-dated local news stories (2020, 2021, 2026) about different specific hamlets. It is not one comprehensive, current, state-wide connectivity survey -- no such single document was found this session. The 2026 Attappady power-outage report in particular comes from one outlet this repo is not familiar with and could not corroborate against a second source; it is included because it is the most current item found. Its inclusion does not mean it is as well-confirmed as the 2021 Onmanorama report. A separate, unresolved tension noted in this session's research (not fully reconciled here) is that a 2015 Government of India press release describes Idukki district as the first in India with complete rural broadband coverage via a national pilot, which sits oddly next to later (2021-2023) reports of tribal colonies within Idukki still lacking internet -- this repo could not find a source explaining that apparent gap and is not asserting either claim supersedes the other.

provenance.contributor_notes: The Madamkunnu (Onmanorama) and Nilambur/Attappady PVTG (The Caravan, The News Minute) articles were fetched and read directly this session. The 2026 Attappady power-outage report was read directly but from a single, less-established outlet and is flagged as needing a second source. District-wide figures quoted inside some of these articles (e.g. "23,000 of ~26,000 Wayanad tribal students lack tablets/laptops," "30 hamlets with no internet") are themselves stated by the articles without a cited government source, so are presented here only as reported. They are not this repo's own confirmed figures.

india-lpm.title: Department of General Education, Government of Kerala

content.label: Department of General Education, Government of Kerala
content.role: Kerala's state education department -- the literal Government of Kerala department that SCERT Kerala (INLP-ACTOR-scert-kerala) operates inside, and the entity actually named as copyright holder on Kerala's own textbooks ("© Department of General Education, Government of Kerala," read directly from the Class 10 Biology textbook's own imprint page). This matters for the same reason NCERT/CBSE's legal form matters nationally: a literal government department asserting copyright is a more straightforward "government work" case under Copyright Act 1957 Section 2(k) than a registered society's claim is -- the opposite kind of legal question from NCERT's, not the same one restated at state level.
content.legalForm: a department of the Government of Kerala itself, not a separate registered society -- confirmed by SCERT Kerala's own self-description as 'an autonomous body of the Department,' not a body standing apart from it, and by the textbook imprint naming the Department, not SCERT, as copyright holder.

provenance.contributor_notes: Confirmed by direct reads of scert.kerala.gov.in's own "about" pages (all describing SCERT as "an autonomous body of the Department of General Education, Government of Kerala") and the Class 10 Biology textbook's own copyright-imprint page (both volumes, 2019 edition, read directly from samagra.kite.kerala.gov.in). No government order or gazette notification establishing SCERT's precise legal instrument was found -- the "department, not a society" reading rests on consistent public self-description plus the textbook's own imprint, not a single definitive legal-instrument document.

india-lpm.title: Scheduled Tribes Development Department, Government of Kerala

content.label: Scheduled Tribes Development Department, Government of Kerala
content.role: Kerala's own line department for Scheduled Tribe welfare and education -- a separate department from the Department of General Education (INLP-ACTOR-dept-general-education-kerala). It is not a unit inside that department. It directly runs Kerala's Model Residential Schools, Ashram Schools, and a pre-metric/post-metric hostel network specifically for Scheduled Tribe students, through a set of Integrated Tribal Development Project (ITDP) and Tribal Development offices around the state (reported locations include Attappady/Agaly, Wayanad/Kalpetta, Idukki/Thodupuzha, and Nilambur). This is the department this founding pass could least directly verify: its own site (stdd.kerala.gov.in) refused every automated fetch attempt this session, so specific counts attributed to it below (how many schools, how many hostels, how many ITDP offices) come from a search tool's summary of that page rather than a character-by-character read, and the specific numbers differ somewhat between different secondary sources that cite it.

provenance.contributor_notes: The department's existence, its ITDP/Tribal Development office structure, and its role running Model Residential/Ashram/Eklavya schools and hostels are corroborated across several independent academic sources (the IRTC/Kerala State Planning Board report on Model Residential Schools, which this repo's INLP-EVENT-emrs-pookode-established-1997 and coherence-finding records draw on directly) as well as its own separate ITDP- Attappady subdomain (itdpattappady.kerala.gov.in), which loaded independently even when the main stdd.kerala.gov.in domain did not. The *exact current* counts (one search summary said "20 MRS/Ashram/Eklavya schools plus 3 hostels," another said "111 hostels serving ~6,000 students" with a different school count) are genuinely inconsistent across sources found this session and should be reconciled by someone who can load the live government page directly before being quoted as a precise figure to an outside reviewer.

india-lpm.title: Kerala Infrastructure and Technology for Education (KITE)

content.label: Kerala Infrastructure and Technology for Education (KITE)
content.role: The technology arm of Kerala's Department of General Education -- began life as the "IT@School Project" in 2001 and was converted into a government-owned company (KITE) in August 2017. Builds and runs the state's own digital-learning infrastructure directly relevant to this project's offline-access question: the Samagra e-Resource Portal (digital textbooks and teacher material for Classes 1-12, jointly run with SCERT), the KITE VICTERS educational TV channel, and the "First Bell" programme built on top of it. Reports serving over 16,000 schools and having deployed more than 4.5 lakh pieces of ICT equipment, with roughly 300 staff across a state office and 14 district offices -- figures are the department's own self-reported scale. This repo has not independently audited them.
content.legalForm: a government-owned company, converted from the earlier IT@School Project in August 2017. It is not a government department itself.

provenance.contributor_notes: Organizational history, scale figures, and the Samagra/VICTERS/ First Bell product set were read directly from KITE's own "Functions and Duties" page. The Samagra portal's own site (samagra.kite.kerala.gov.in) returned almost no extractable text to this session's tools, so the specific claim that Samagra offers a genuine offline-download option (as opposed to being view-only online) rests on third-party aggregator sites repeating each other. This repo has not read Samagra's own site to confirm it directly -- flagged for that direct confirmation before being treated as a solved part of the offline-access question this project cares about most.

india-lpm.title: Kerala Institute for Research, Training and Development Studies of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (KIRTADS)

content.label: Kerala Institute for Research, Training and Development Studies of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (KIRTADS)
content.role: A Government of Kerala research institute in Chevayur, near Kozhikode, founded in 1972 as the Tribal Research and Training Centre and renamed KIRTADS in 1979. Runs Training, Research, and Development Studies wings plus an Ethnological Museum (established 1973) documenting Scheduled Caste/Scheduled Tribe material culture. Directly relevant to this project because KIRTADS is the body credited with producing Kerala's bilingual Malayalam-Paniya bridge primers for early-grade tribal students (a Paniya Language Primer Part II for Standard I, 2018, and Part III for Standard II, completed April 2021, both authored by Dr. S. Bindu) -- one of the few concrete, named examples found this session of a Kerala government body producing tribal-language classroom material. Most of what else this session found is Malayalam-medium content alone.

provenance.contributor_notes: Institutional history read directly from KIRTADS' own site and cross-checked against independent Wikipedia coverage (including a named former director, P.R.G. Mathur), which agree. The Paniya primer bibliographic details (exact author, year, grade level) come from a Ministry of Tribal Affairs digital-repository listing this session could not open directly (404 error) -- KIRTADS' own existence and general role are solid; the specific primer titles and dates should be re-confirmed by opening https://repository.tribal.gov.in/handle/123456789/75212 directly.

india-lpm.title: Samagra Shiksha Kerala (SSK)

content.label: Samagra Shiksha Kerala (SSK)
content.role: Kerala's implementing wing of the central Samagra Shiksha Abhiyan scheme -- described in sourcing found this session as "the state's school-education mission." This is the body repeatedly named as the implementer behind Kerala's COVID-era mother-tongue bridge-content efforts for tribal students (reported under at least two different names in different outlets -- see INLP-EVENT-covid-era-tribal-mother-tongue-bridge-content-2020, which flags that naming inconsistency directly rather than picking one) and the Gothrabandhu tribal mentor-teacher programme (INLP-EVENT-gothrabandhu-mentor-teacher-program-launched-2017), and also the body that designed Edamalakudy's "Padippurasi" bridge workshop for Muthuvan children specifically (named staff: CA Shameer, a Government Tribal Lower Primary School teacher; Bindumol D, SSK's Idukki district project officer; TP Kaladharan, an SSK educational consultant).

provenance.contributor_notes: SSK's role is consistently named across several independently fetched news articles (Careers360, The News Minute, Outlook India, The Caravan) describing different specific programmes, which gives reasonable confidence in its existence and general role, but no SSK-specific "about us" government page was read directly this session to confirm its exact administrative structure or current (2026) staffing/scope.

india-lpm.title: State Council of Educational Research and Training (SCERT), Kerala

content.label: State Council of Educational Research and Training (SCERT), Kerala
content.role: Kerala's state curriculum-research body -- publishes the Kerala Curriculum Framework (most recently KCF 2023, succeeding a 2007 version built on stated critical-pedagogy/issue-based/social- constructivist foundations, explicitly positioned by Kerala's Education Department as a state-level alternative to NEP 2020 rather than an implementation of it) and Kerala's own state textbooks. Unlike Karnataka's DSERT, SCERT Kerala has no confirmed open license on its own curriculum text or textbooks -- its Class 10 Biology textbook's copyright page carries a bare copyright notice only, no Creative Commons mark or stated reuse permission, and the same is true of the KCF 2023 landing page itself. No KOER-equivalent open platform was found in Kerala's own education-technology ecosystem (IT@School/KITE's open-source commitment covers software/ infrastructure, not a license on curriculum text; the Samagra portal is a plain PDF-distribution site with no license statement; School Wiki's own license could not be confirmed, site unreachable this session).

provenance.contributor_notes: SCERT's own "about" self-description, the KCF 2023 landing page, and the Samagra portal were all read directly, as was the Class 10 Biology textbook's own copyright-imprint page. The critical- pedagogy/constructivist framing is well-corroborated for KCF generally (multiple independent secondary sources) but was not independently confirmed from the KCF 2023 document's own primary text this session (its direct download link was not reachable) -- treat that specific continuity claim as very likely, not verified.

india-lpm.title: Kerala directs schools to keep teaching evolution content NCERT deleted nationally

content.label: Kerala directs schools to keep teaching evolution content NCERT deleted nationally
content.description: Following NCERT's 2023-2024 national "rationalisation" exercise, which deleted entire chapters on Darwin's theory of evolution (along with Mughal-history and caste-system content) from national textbooks, Kerala's Chief Minister publicly criticized the deletions and SCERT Kerala directed state schools to continue teaching the removed content, releasing its own supplementary textbooks and forming a review committee. This is a curriculum-content dispute, not a copyright dispute -- Kerala is not asserting a licensing claim here, it is rejecting a national content decision on substantive grounds. Filed as its own event rather than folded into the licensing-history events above because it is a different kind of fact, directly relevant to this project's own evolution-education focus: a real instance of a state-level body actively defending evolution content against removal, not a hypothetical concern.
content.licenseOrRightsNote: Paraphrased from news coverage (careers360.com reporting on Kerala CM/SCERT statements), not a verbatim reproduction of any curriculum text or official notification.

provenance.contributor_notes: Confirmed via direct reads of two careers360.com news articles ("Kerala CM releases supplementary textbooks; attacks NCERT over removal of portions" and "Kerala schools likely to teach deleted parts of NCERT history, social science textbooks: SCERT"). News coverage, not a primary government order or SCERT notification -- treat the exact sequence/dates as approximate pending a primary source. See INLP-EVENT-ncert-rationalisation-evolution-deletion (national timeline) for the deletion this responds to, and state/kerala/local_policy/records/coherence-findings.yaml for how Kerala's own retained content compares in actual depth.

india-lpm.license_or_rights_note: Paraphrased from news coverage (careers360.com reporting on Kerala CM/SCERT statements), not a verbatim reproduction of any curriculum text or official notification.

india-lpm.title: Kerala Curriculum Framework (KCF) 2007 adopted

content.label: Kerala Curriculum Framework (KCF) 2007 adopted
content.description: SCERT Kerala adopted its first Kerala Curriculum Framework (KCF) as a continuation of the National Curriculum Framework (NCF) 2005. KCF 2023's own foreword states the later framework "builds upon the foundation laid by" this 2007 version, and names the shared pedagogical commitment directly: "critical pedagogy and social constructivism as formulated by Vygotsky... had received cardinal importance in the Kerala Curriculum Framework [2007]," alongside issue-based learning. This repo has not located or read the original 2007 document itself (only KCF 2023's own description of it, plus an independent peer-reviewed case study corroborating the same characterization) -- see the coherence-finding and principle records this event grounds for what that pedagogical stance does and does not extend to.
content.licenseOrRightsNote: Summarized from KCF 2023's own description of its predecessor and from an independent peer-reviewed secondary source. This is not from a direct read of the 2007 document itself.

provenance.contributor_notes: The critical-pedagogy/social-constructivist/issue-based characterization is independently corroborated by Vishnu Prakash Kareepadath, "Critical Pedagogy in Practice: A Case Study from Kerala, India," Journal of Pedagogy, 9(2), 33-54 (2018), a peer-reviewed source examining how Kerala teachers actually practiced this stance in classrooms. No exact adoption date (only "2007") was confirmed, and this repo has not read the original KCF 2007 PDF directly -- only KCF 2023's retrospective description of it.

india-lpm.license_or_rights_note: Summarized from KCF 2023's own description of its predecessor and from an independent peer-reviewed secondary source. This is not from a direct read of the 2007 document itself.

india-lpm.title: Kerala Curriculum Framework (KCF) 2023 adopted, explicitly as a state-level alternative to NEP 2020

content.label: Kerala Curriculum Framework (KCF) 2023 adopted, explicitly as a state-level alternative to NEP 2020
content.description: SCERT Kerala published KCF 2023, produced by a Core Committee on Curriculum Reform (convened by SCERT's Director, chaired by the Principal Secretary for General Education) using 26 thematic focus groups and public consultations the document says involved over 30 lakh students. Read directly from the official 223-page English PDF: the document states plainly that "the National Education Policy of 2020 does not put forward the same perspective that was presented in the first policy on school education... The federal system of the constitution has given space to all the states to take a position that caters to the specific needs of the state" -- i.e. Kerala frames KCF 2023 as a deliberate state-level alternative to NEP 2020. It is not framed as an implementation of NEP 2020. News coverage adds that this includes rejecting NEP's 5+3+3+4 school-stage structure for Kerala's own (reported as 3+7+5), while keeping scientific temper, secularism and constitutional values -- 173 new KCF-aligned textbooks reportedly open with the Constitution's Preamble. KCF 2023 explicitly names Scheduled Tribe children as a group needing "special care and support" and mandates a "Tribal Education Committee" as a required sub-section of each local Panchayat Education Committee -- but a full-text search of the English PDF found no mention of any specific tribal community, tribal language, Wayanad or Attappady by name in a current tribal-policy context, residential/hostel schooling, or a dedicated curricular unit on tribal/indigenous local knowledge; its one use of "local knowledge" is a general statement about strengthening the regional economy. It is not a tribal-education-specific goal. See INLP-FINDING-kcf2023-names-tribal-equity-but-omits-tribal-specifics for the full analysis.
content.licenseOrRightsNote: Summarized/paraphrased from the official KCF 2023 PDF and from news coverage of it -- the one directly quoted sentence above (on NEP 2020) is a short excerpt used for precise, checkable attribution. It is not a substitute for the document itself, and no attempt is made here to reproduce the document at length.

provenance.contributor_notes: This record is a genuine upgrade over this repo's earlier INLP-ACTOR-scert-kerala note (2026-10-02), which could not reach KCF 2023's own text directly and flagged the critical-pedagogy continuity claim as "very likely, not verified" -- this session downloaded and full-text-searched the actual 223-page English PDF linked from SCERT Kerala's own site. The "3+7+5" structure and the 173-textbook/Preamble detail rest on news coverage (The Federal, Careers360). They are not confirmed inside the PDF text itself. The negative finding (no named tribal community/language/district in the document) is a careful absence-of-evidence finding from the English edition only -- it does not rule out the Malayalam edition, subject-specific syllabi, or textbooks carrying such content, and should not be presented to an outside reviewer as proof the state curriculum ignores tribal communities. The only supported claim is that this particular framework document's English text does not name them.

india-lpm.title: Kerala launches "First Bell" televised/virtual classes in response to COVID-19 school closures

content.label: Kerala launches "First Bell" televised/virtual classes in response to COVID-19 school closures
content.description: KITE VICTERS (Kerala's educational TV channel) launched "First Bell" on 1 June 2020 for grades 1-12 plus a pre-primary strand ("Kilikkonchal") -- a live broadcast on the free VICTERS channel, re-uploaded same-day to YouTube, also reachable via the KITE VICTERS app/site and social media. A "First Bell 2.0" followed on 1 June 2021. Directly relevant to this project because First Bell is a live-broadcast-plus-streaming model. It is not a store-and-forward, offline-first one. For students with neither a TV nor internet, Kerala's documented response was organizational rather than technical: "Neighbourhood Study Centres" with subsidized TVs in public buildings, and a public device-donation drive. A 2020 government survey reportedly found about 261,000 students (roughly 6% of the government-school population) had no device to view First Bell at all; a two-week mobilization drive cut this to about 17,774 children still needing access by the time term began. Separately, reporting from the same period describes Kerala translating First Bell's Class 1 content into tribal dialects for an estimated 25,000 tribal Class 1 students, under a program named inconsistently across sources -- see INLP-EVENT-covid-era-tribal-mother-tongue-bridge-content-2020.

india-lpm.title: Samagra Shiksha Kerala translates First Bell / produces mother-tongue video lessons for tribal students during COVID-19 closures

content.label: Samagra Shiksha Kerala translates First Bell / produces mother-tongue video lessons for tribal students during COVID-19 closures
content.description: During 2020 COVID-19 school closures, Samagra Shiksha Kerala (SSK) produced mother-tongue video lessons for tribal Class 1 students, distributed via a dedicated YouTube channel, WhatsApp parent groups, and community-centre televisions, with mother-tongue mentor teachers from the same communities preparing/recording lessons. This repo found the effort described under two different names in independent news coverage, with inconsistent scope details, and is deliberately recording that inconsistency rather than resolving it by guessing: one report (Outlook India, naming SSA Director Dr. A.P. Kuttikrishnan) calls it "Namath Basai," piloted first in Attappady (Irula, Muduka, Kurumba languages) and extended to Wayanad and Idukki, covering six languages (Kattunayikka, Paniya, Adiya, Kurichiya, Oorali, Kuruma) with 241 teachers and 60 volunteers in Wayanad alone; another report (The News Minute) calls a July 2020 Wayanad-area effort "Mazhavil Poovu," translating Class 1 First Bell lessons for about 25,000 students, with differing counts elsewhere of six vs. ten dialects/communities covered. These may be the same programme described inconsistently by different outlets, or two related but distinct efforts -- this repo could not resolve which from the sources read this session.

india-lpm.title: "Gothrabandhu" tribal mentor-teacher programme launched

content.label: "Gothrabandhu" tribal mentor-teacher programme launched
content.description: Samagra Shiksha Kerala launched "Gothrabandhu" in the 2017-18 academic year: locally recruited, tribal-background mentor-teachers fluent in Malayalam and a local tribal dialect, placed into primary schools with tribal students specifically to reduce dropout and address the language barrier between home language and Malayalam- medium instruction. content.label: Maharashtra State Bureau of Textbook Production and Curriculum Research (Balbharati)
content.role: Maharashtra's state textbook-publishing and curriculum-research bureau. florida-lpm.title: Standards that name a contested concept explicitly are more durable than standards that gesture at it euphemistically

content.label: Standards that name a contested concept explicitly are more durable than standards that gesture at it euphemistically
content.statement: When a curriculum standard avoids naming a scientifically settled but politically contested concept directly -- using a vaguer substitute phrase instead of the term itself -- that avoidance does not resolve the underlying political pressure; it just defers the fight to the next revision cycle, at a cost paid by whichever cohort of students sits between editions. Florida's own record is the clearest evidence for this available anywhere in this ecosystem: standards that avoided "evolution" (pre-2008) were graded academically unsound by name; the standards that then explicitly named it, even in hedged form, held for eighteen years; and the current proposal to drop explicit naming again is being criticized in the same terms the 2005 Fordham review used against the pre-2008 standards. A standards body gains nothing durable by euphemism -- only a shorter interval before the same argument recurs.
content.rationale: This is not a claim that explicit naming settles the underlying political disagreement -- it doesn't, and Florida's 2008 compromise ("the scientific theory of evolution") shows a state can name a concept explicitly while still hedging around it. The claim is narrower and empirical: avoidance is not even a stable truce. It is simply the shortest-lived of the three postures a standards document can take (avoid, hedge, name plainly), based on the one case this ecosystem has tracked across four decades.

florida-lpm.title: A standards-writing committee needs disciplinary experts proportionate to what it is writing standards for

content.label: A standards-writing committee needs disciplinary experts proportionate to what it is writing standards for
content.statement: A committee asked to write K-12 science standards should include enough working scientists and science educators that the document's scientific framing is actually load-bearing in the room, not a single voice outnumbered seventeen to one. Florida's 2026 draft was written by an 18-person committee with exactly one science-education professional on it -- the rest school-district employees -- at the same time FLDOE reportedly has no K-12 science specialists on its own staff. This is a staffing-composition fact, independent of what the resulting standards actually say, and it is a predictable risk factor for exactly the kind of gap (a 1,000-benchmark document a national science-education organization calls "a mile wide and an inch deep") that followed.
content.rationale: This principle deliberately stops short of asserting the committee composition CAUSED the specific omissions reported in the 2026 draft -- that causal claim isn't something this repo's research established, and asserting it would overstate what's actually known. What IS established is the staffing fact itself, confirmed by FLDOE's own named officials (Patricia Duncan, Alicia Foy). A review process this thin on subject-matter expertise is a structural risk condition worth naming on its own terms.

florida-lpm.title: A well-documented, decades-long curriculum controversy is itself legitimate classroom content, not just background politics to route around

content.label: A well-documented, decades-long curriculum controversy is itself legitimate classroom content, not just background politics to route around
content.statement: Florida's own evolution-standards history -- a real, four-decade, multiply-recurring public fight over what a state is willing to name in its own science standards -- is a concrete, well-sourced case study in how scientific consensus, institutional governance, and organized public pressure actually interact. Rather than treating this history as noise to be kept out of the classroom, a curriculum designed around OpenEvo's Nature of Science and civic-reasoning goals can use Florida's own documented record (who took which position, what changed, what didn't) as a worked example of how a real governing body resolves -- or fails to resolve -- a contested empirical question under public pressure, distinct from and in addition to teaching the underlying biology itself.
content.rationale: This is the practical payoff of building policy-controversy-record in the first place: once a controversy is modeled as a structured record (named positions, real press coverage, a tracked outcome) rather than left as prose, it becomes something a curriculum designer can actually build a lesson or discussion unit from, not just background context a teacher has to research independently.

florida-lpm.title: Florida's standards shifted from avoiding the word "evolution" (pre-2008) to explicitly naming it (2008)

content.label: Florida's standards shifted from avoiding the word "evolution" (pre-2008) to explicitly naming it (2008)

objects.policyArea: NGSSS SC.912.L.15 (2008, still in force through 2020)
objects.sourceDocument: Next Generation Sunshine State Standards (NGSSS), Science

florida-lpm.title: The 2026 draft standards omit explicit naming of both "evolution" and "climate change," reversing 2008's explicit-naming approach

content.label: The 2026 draft standards omit explicit naming of both "evolution" and "climate change," reversing 2008's explicit-naming approach

florida-lpm.title: The 2008 fight over explicitly naming evolution in the Next Generation Sunshine State Standards

content.label: The 2008 fight over explicitly naming evolution in the Next Generation Sunshine State Standards
content.topicArea: Whether Florida's science standards should explicitly name "evolution" at all, and if so, whether the word must be qualified by "the scientific theory of."
content.summary: FLDOE's October 2007 draft standards were the first in Florida's history to explicitly use the word "evolution." Organized religious-right opposition (Focus on the Family, the Florida Baptist Witness, the Florida Family Policy Council, at least 12 county school boards) pushed back through late 2007, while Florida Citizens for Science led a public counter-campaign defending the draft, backed by the National Academy of Sciences and other scientific bodies. Days before the Feb 19, 2008 vote, under pressure, the State Board had the draft redrafted to insert "the scientific theory of" before "evolution" as a last-minute compromise, which the Board then adopted 4-3.
content.outcomeSummary: The State Board adopted the standards with "the scientific theory of" qualifier inserted before "evolution" (and before several other scientific theories/laws) -- the first explicit naming of evolution in Florida's standards, but in a hedged form that satisfied neither side fully: opponents wanted evolution presented as contestable, while board member Roberto Martinez and the original writing committee considered the qualifier an unnecessary, "watered down" concession.

contestedObjects.description: Whether SC.912.L.15 and related benchmarks should name "evolution" explicitly, and whether that name should be qualified by "the scientific theory of."

positions.actorLabel: Florida Citizens for Science (Brandon Haught, co-founder)
positions.stanceSummary: Defended the original draft's unqualified use of "evolution," organized a 1,700+-signature petition, and called the adopted compromise "a huge step forward for our Florida schools" despite the hedged wording.
Organized opposition to the draft's explicit naming of evolution, part of the same push that led to the 2008 "Academic Freedom Act" legislative fight.

positions.actorLabel: Roberto Martinez (Florida State Board of Education member)
positions.stanceSummary: Voted NO on the adopted compromise -- not because he opposed naming evolution, but because he considered the late "scientific theory of" qualifier an unnecessary watering-down of the original, scientifically stronger draft the National Academy of Sciences had endorsed: "What we have here is an effort by people to water down our standards."

positions.actorLabel: Donna Callaway (Florida State Board of Education member)
positions.stanceSummary: Voted NO on the adopted compromise from the opposite direction, having pushed for a further "critical analysis" amendment to the evolution standard that did not pass.

florida-lpm.title: The 2008 "Academic Freedom Act" (SB 2692/HB 1483) legislative fight

content.label: The 2008 "Academic Freedom Act" (SB 2692/HB 1483) legislative fight
content.topicArea: Whether Florida law should require "critical analysis" of evolution be taught alongside it, via a Discovery-Institute-template "Academic Freedom Act."
content.summary: Running concurrently with the NGSSS standards fight, Sen. Ronda Storms and Rep. Alan Hays introduced companion bills modeled on Discovery Institute's template "Academic Freedom Act" legislation (the same template Louisiana enacted in June 2008 and Tennessee enacted in 2012). The House passed a substituted version 71-43, but the Senate rejected the substitution and the bill died in a standoff at the end of the 2008 session.
content.outcomeSummary: The bill died without becoming law -- the House and Senate could not agree on which chamber's version to send to the Governor, and the session ended with no further action. florida-lpm.title: 2017-2018 textbook challenges against evolution/climate content under HB 989

content.label: 2017-2018 textbook challenges against evolution/climate content under HB 989
content.topicArea: Whether specific adopted science textbooks' treatment of evolution and/or human-caused climate change should be removed, stickered, or otherwise altered, using HB 989's any-resident-may-object mechanism.
content.summary: Within months of HB 989 taking effect, residents in at least three Florida counties (Nassau, Collier, Martin) filed formal objections specifically targeting evolution and/or climate-change content in adopted science textbooks. Nassau County's objection (the first statewide) sought disclaimer stickers; it and the Collier/Martin County objections were all rejected at the school-board level, but the mechanism itself remained in place for future use.
content.outcomeSummary: All three known 2017-18 evolution/climate-specific challenges failed at the school-board vote stage (Nassau's sticker proposal voted down; Collier and Martin both failed 3-2) -- the original textbooks were retained unaltered in every case. Florida Citizens for Science reports at least 7 total instructional-materials complaints statewide in HB 989's first 5 months, of which at least 2 specifically targeted evolution/climate content.

florida-lpm.title: The 2026 fight over omitting "evolution" and "climate change" from Florida's first science-standards rewrite since 2008

content.label: The 2026 fight over omitting "evolution" and "climate change" from Florida's first science-standards rewrite since 2008
content.topicArea: Whether Florida's proposed 2026 K-12 science standards -- which do not use the word "evolution" in high-school life-science content, and do not use "climate change"/"global warming" anywhere -- should be revised before adoption, and what the omissions mean about the state's intent.
content.summary: FLDOE's draft rewrite (the first full science-standards revision since 2008) removes explicit naming of both evolution and climate change, drawing fierce, wide-ranging criticism from teachers, a science specialist, the state teachers' union, and the National Center for Science Education, while FLDOE's own leadership defends the draft as still substantively covering the underlying science. As of this record's provenance date, the dispute is active: a public-comment listening tour is underway and a State Board vote is expected December 2026.

contestedObjects.description: Whether the 2026 draft's omission of the word "evolution" from high-school life-science standards, and of "climate change"/"global warming" from the entire document, should be corrected before the State Board's expected December 2026 vote.

positions.stanceSummary: Defended the draft as substantively covering evolution and climate science despite the wording concerns: "We want evolutionary biology in the standards, they are in the standards... My kids are reading Charles Darwin"; "We are teaching climate science... Sea level rise is in the standards." Separately described the draft's philosophy in explicitly classical/teleological terms: "Science begins in wonder, not in ideology... Florida's new standards will form students who observe carefully, reason rigorously, and treat the natural world as something given to be known, not invented."
Told a public listening session the omissions were "not intentional," and that the listening tour was "the first of many steps."

"I would like to say something nice about the new standards, but I can't." Criticized the draft's ~1,000 high-school benchmarks as "a mile wide and an inch deep," much of it "fun-fact-style trivia" rather than a teaching framework.

positions.actorLabel: Bertha Vazquez (Director, Teacher Institute for Evolutionary Science)
positions.stanceSummary: "Moving backward... If it's not broken, why the hell are we fixing it? We had smash bang good standards."
"Evolution is a fundamental underlying process unifying all of biology. To leave it out is ideology posing as biology."

positions.actorLabel: Lindsey Craven (Science Specialist, grades 9-12, Pinellas County Schools)
positions.stanceSummary: Noted the standards "reference... evolution without actually... stating evolution."
Warned that teaching outside mainstream science leaves Florida students "at a disadvantage," and formally requested extended review periods and additional virtual town halls.

florida-lpm.title: Florida State Board of Education votes 4-3 to adopt the Next Generation Sunshine State Standards

content.label: Florida State Board of Education votes 4-3 to adopt the Next Generation Sunshine State Standards
content.description: Days before the vote, under public and legislative pressure, Education Commissioner Eric Smith redrafted the standards to insert "the scientific theory of" before "evolution" (and before plate tectonics, cell theory, atomic theory, electromagnetism, and "scientific law of" before gravity) -- a late compromise ("Option B"). A further amendment proposed by board member Donna Callaway calling for "critical analysis" of evolution did NOT pass. The Board voted 4-3 to adopt the compromise version: YES -- T. Willard Fair (Chairman), Linda Taylor, Kathleen Shanahan, Phoebe Raulerson. NO -- Roberto Martinez (opposing because the compromise watered down the original, scientifically stronger draft, which the National Academy of Sciences had endorsed), Akshay Desai, Donna Callaway (opposing from the other direction, wanting weaker language than even the compromise). This was Florida's first standards document to explicitly name "evolution."

florida-lpm.title: SB 2692 / HB 1483 "Academic Freedom Act" introduced, passes House, dies in Senate standoff

content.label: SB 2692 / HB 1483 "Academic Freedom Act" introduced, passes House, dies in Senate standoff
content.description: Sen. Ronda Storms (R-Valrico) introduced SB 2692 following Discovery Institute's model "Academic Freedom Act" statute; Rep. Alan Hays introduced the House companion HB 1483, narrowed to call for "thorough presentation and critical analysis of the scientific theory of evolution." John Stemberger (Florida Family Policy Council) was lead public advocate. Hays hosted a closed March 2008 press event with a Discovery Institute representative, for legislators only. The House passed its substituted version (HB 1483 text swapped into SB 2692) 71-43 on April 28, 2008; the Senate rejected the substitution and restored its own text, sending it back to the House, which left it untouched -- the bill died at session's end without becoming law. This is the same Discovery Institute template later enacted in Louisiana (June 2008) and Tennessee (2012), but Florida's version did not pass.

pennsylvania-lpm.title: A state standard requiring evolution be taught does not, by itself, prevent a local district from undermining it

content.label: A state standard requiring evolution be taught does not, by itself, prevent a local district from undermining it
content.statement: Pennsylvania's own state science standard required students to "analyze the theory of evolution" years before Dover's board required a disclaimer suggesting the theory has unresolved "gaps/problems" and promoting "intelligent design" as an alternative. The state's own requirement did neither cause nor prevent the district's policy -- a well-worded state standard is necessary but not sufficient protection against a local curriculum mandate that goes further than the state ever authorized. A curriculum-policy archive that only tracks state- level standards would have missed the entire Dover story, which happened one level down.
content.rationale: This is the direct, practical lesson of building district-vs-state-standard-divergence as its own finding type: the interesting and consequential curriculum politics in a region are not always where the state-level authority sits. Florida's own case (florida-lpm) is the inverse: there, the state authority itself was the site of the fight. Both are real, and a repository that only modeled one level would be systematically blind to half of what actually happens in curriculum politics.

pennsylvania-lpm.title: A court ruling can settle a curriculum dispute more durably than a subsequent vote, where a constitutional question is actually at stake

content.label: A court ruling can settle a curriculum dispute more durably than a subsequent vote, where a constitutional question is actually at stake
content.statement: Florida's 2008 compromise over "the scientific theory of evolution" was a negotiated wording that satisfied neither side fully and left the same underlying question open to recur in 2026. Pennsylvania's Dover case was resolved differently: a federal court found the specific constitutional question (whether the policy was religiously motivated) as a matter of fact and law, not as a negotiated compromise -- and eighteen years later, no comparable Pennsylvania evolution-standards controversy has recurred, where Florida's has. A dispute that genuinely raises a constitutional question is a different kind of dispute than a disagreement over standards wording, and the two should not be expected to resolve the same way or with the same durability.
content.rationale: This is a direct, evidence-based comparison across two repos built in the same session -- not a general claim that litigation is always better than politics. Most curriculum disputes (Florida's, most of Pennsylvania's own 2002 standards fight) never raise a genuine constitutional question and have no litigation path available; this principle applies narrowly to the subset that do.

pennsylvania-lpm.title: Teachers refusing to implement a mandate they judge unscientific is itself a documentable form of curriculum governance

content.label: Teachers refusing to implement a mandate they judge unscientific is itself a documentable form of curriculum governance
content.statement: All eight of Dover's biology teachers formally refused to read the district's disclaimer, citing their profession's own ethics code -- not a lawsuit, not a vote, but a collective act of professional judgment that forced the district to have administrators read it instead, visibly separating the policy from the people actually teaching the subject. This is a real, recordable check on curriculum governance distinct from litigation, elections, or standards text itself, and a curriculum-politics archive should have a place to record it as a historical fact (here, as part of PALP-EVENT-dover-teachers-refuse-and-disclaimer-first-read), not only as color in a narrative.
content.rationale: Worth naming as its own principle because none of this ecosystem's existing record types (institutional-actor, mandate, controversy position) are quite built around "a profession's own collective refusal to implement" as a category -- it currently lives as a timeline event and a controversy position, which works, but a future session building out more teacher-driven curriculum-resistance cases (a real, recurring category in US curriculum politics) might find it worth a more explicit modeling treatment than this repo attempted.

pennsylvania-lpm.title: PA's 2002 standard changed from "support or do not support" to "relevant to" the theory of evolution after public pressure

content.policyRelevance: Establishes that Pennsylvania had a real, document-level fight over evolution-standard wording nearly five years before the Dover case reached federal court -- the state-level and district-level episodes are related but distinct, not the same event retold.

pennsylvania-lpm.title: Dover's district policy went well beyond what Pennsylvania's own state standard required or permitted

content.label: Dover's district policy went well beyond what Pennsylvania's own state standard required or permitted

objects.policyArea: PA state standard 3.3.10.D (2002, in force during the Dover dispute)
objects.excerptText: analyze the theory of evolution

objects.policyArea: Dover Area School District's 2004 curriculum policy
objects.excerptText: Students will be made aware of gaps/problems in Darwin's theory and of other theories of evolution including, but not limited to, intelligent design.
objects.sourceDocument: Dover Area School Board meeting minutes / Kitzmiller trial exhibit

content.summary: Pennsylvania's own state standard required analyzing the theory of evolution and said nothing about "gaps/problems" or alternative "theories" including intelligent design -- language the State Board had specifically revised away from in its own 2002 rulemaking (see PALP-FINDING-pa-2002-proposed-vs-final-wording-change). Dover's district policy introduced exactly the kind of framing the state had already rejected, at the district level, two years later, citing "the state standards" as its own justification even though the state standard did not call for or permit this content.
content.policyRelevance: This is the direct textual basis for understanding Kitzmiller v. Dover as a story about a district exceeding an already-adequate state standard, not about a weak or ambiguous state standard needing correction -- NCSE's own later grading of PA's evolution standards as "A" (2009, 2017) is consistent with this finding, not in tension with it.
content.exhaustivenessCaveat: Based on the characterizations of both documents available this session; the complete verbatim 3.3.10.D descriptor beyond "analyze the theory of evolution" was not independently re-confirmed.

provenance.sourceProvenance: Pennsylvania Bulletin Vol. 32 Issue 1; NCSE's Kitzmiller coverage -- both fetched and read directly.

pennsylvania-lpm.title: Unlike Florida's 2026 rewrite, evolution content was not the point of controversy in PA's 2019-2022 standards revision

content.label: Unlike Florida's 2026 rewrite, evolution content was not the point of controversy in PA's 2019-2022 standards revision
content.summary: NCSE-commissioned reviews graded Pennsylvania's 2002 standards "A" for both high-school (2009) and middle-school (2017) evolution content, but "F" for climate-change content (2020) -- and it was specifically the climate-change grade that drove public comment and debate during the 2019-2022 STEELS revision (e.g. climate scientist Michael Mann's public critique of a draft version, June 2021), not evolution.
content.policyRelevance: A direct contrast with florida-lpm's 2026 case, where evolution WAS the center of public controversy over a contemporaneous standards rewrite. Pennsylvania's evolution-education story is centered entirely on the 2004-2006 Dover district-level episode; its state-level standards have not been a site of evolution-specific controversy before or since.
content.exhaustivenessCaveat: Based on NCSE's own published grading reports and its June 2021 article on the STEELS draft, checked specifically for an evolution angle (none found) -- not a systematic review of every public comment submitted during the 2019-2022 process.

pennsylvania-lpm.title: The pre-Dover 2000-2002 fight over how PA's first evolution-naming standard should be worded

content.label: The pre-Dover 2000-2002 fight over how PA's first evolution-naming standard should be worded
content.topicArea: Whether Pennsylvania's first science standard to explicitly mention evolution should ask students to analyze evidence that "supports or does not support" evolution, or more neutrally, evidence "relevant to" it.
content.summary: During rulemaking for Pennsylvania's 2002 science standards, the proposed wording for the evolution standard was challenged by more than 120 public commenters and the Independent Regulatory Review Commission as effectively inviting creationism/intelligent-design framing into the classroom. The State Board revised the final wording in response, explicitly disclaiming any intent to encourage teaching creationism or intelligent design.
content.outcomeSummary: The State Board adopted the revised, more neutral wording ("relevant to the theory of evolution") rather than the originally proposed language -- the side objecting to the "support or do not support" framing prevailed in the final rulemaking.

contestedObjects.description: Whether Standard 3.3.10.D should ask students to analyze evidence that "supports or does not support" evolution, versus evidence "relevant to" it.

positions.stanceSummary: Raised concern during the rulemaking review that the proposed "support or do not support" wording could invite creationism or intelligent-design framing.

positions.actorLabel: 120+ individual and organizational public commenters (not individually named in sources reviewed)
positions.stanceSummary: Objected that the proposed wording "inappropriately singled out" evolution and could "permit or even encourage schools to teach creationism or intelligent design."
Revised the final wording and stated it "did not intend to encourage the teaching of creationism or intelligent design," framing the standard as "written to encourage critical thinking."

pennsylvania-lpm.title: Kitzmiller v. Dover -- the fight over teaching intelligent design alongside evolution

content.label: Kitzmiller v. Dover -- the fight over teaching intelligent design alongside evolution
content.topicArea: Whether a public school district may require a disclaimer statement presenting "intelligent design" as a scientific alternative to evolution be read to students before the evolution unit.
content.summary: The Dover Area School Board voted 6-3 in October 2004 to require students be told of "gaps/problems" in evolution and of "other theories... including, but not limited to, intelligent design." All eight Dover biology teachers refused to read the resulting disclaimer themselves; eleven parents sued; a six-week federal trial followed; voters ousted every pro-policy board member before the ruling came down; and Judge John E. Jones III ruled the policy unconstitutional, finding intelligent design is not science and is a form of creationism. The new board did not appeal and formally rescinded the policy weeks later.
content.outcomeSummary: The intelligent-design disclaimer policy was both ruled unconstitutional by a federal court (Dec 20, 2005) and formally, unanimously rescinded by the newly elected board (Jan 3, 2006) -- resolved decisively against the change the original 2004 board fought for, not by a subsequent compromise.

contestedObjects.description: Whether Dover's biology curriculum could require students be told of "gaps/problems" in evolution and be directed toward "intelligent design" and the book "Of Pandas and People" as an alternative explanation.

positions.stanceSummary: Led the push to balance evolution with creationism/intelligent design, objecting that the proposed biology textbook was "laced with Darwinism."

positions.actorLabel: Jeffrey and Carol "Casey" Brown (Dover board members, resigned in protest)
positions.stanceSummary: Voted against the policy and resigned immediately afterward. Casey Brown: "it has become increasingly evident that in the direction the board has now chosen to go, holding a certain religious belief is of paramount importance... I can no longer effectively function as a member of this board."

Formally refused to read the disclaimer, stating intelligent design "is not science" and "not an accepted scientific theory," and that reading it would "violate the ethics code of [their] profession."

positions.actorLabel: Tammy Kitzmiller and the 10 other plaintiff parents (represented by Pepper Hamilton LLP, Americans United, ACLU of Pennsylvania)
positions.stanceSummary: Sued to block the policy as an unconstitutional establishment of religion.

positions.actorLabel: Thomas More Law Center (defense counsel for the school board)
positions.stanceSummary: Defended the board's policy at trial as permissible under the Establishment Clause.

Publicly distanced itself from Dover's SPECIFIC policy even while promoting intelligent design generally: its own site states it "repeatedly advised the Dover School Board and [Thomas More Law Center] that the board's intelligent design policy... was problematic and should be replaced," and three of its affiliated fellows who had agreed to serve as defense experts withdrew before depositions.

positions.actorLabel: Kenneth R. Miller (plaintiffs' lead science expert witness, Brown University)
positions.stanceSummary: Testified that intelligent design, including the bacterial- flagellum "irreducible complexity" argument, is not testable science, citing peer-reviewed research on flagellum evolutionary precursors.

positions.actorLabel: Michael Behe (defense expert witness, Lehigh University)
positions.stanceSummary: Testified the bacterial flagellum exhibits "irreducible complexity" that could not have evolved stepwise; under cross-examination conceded there are "no peer reviewed articles by anyone... providing detailed, rigorous accounts of how intelligent design of any biological system occurred," and that his own definition of "theory" was broad enough to include astrology.

positions.actorLabel: Judge John E. Jones III (US District Court, Middle District of Pennsylvania)
positions.stanceSummary: Ruled the policy unconstitutional: intelligent design is not science and is a form of creationism; the board acted with religious intent, violating the Establishment Clause. Wrote that "the breathtaking inanity of the Board's decision is evident when considered against the factual backdrop which has now been fully revealed through this trial," and found board members Buckingham and Bonsell gave false testimony about the policy's religious origins.
positions.licenseOrRightsNote: A federal court's own published opinion is a public judicial record.

pennsylvania-lpm.title: Dover Area School District's 2004 intelligent-design disclaimer policy

content.label: Dover Area School District's 2004 intelligent-design disclaimer policy
content.issuingBody: Dover Area School District Board
content.statementText: [Board policy, adopted 2004-10-18:] "Students will be made aware of gaps/problems in Darwin's theory and of other theories of evolution including, but not limited to, intelligent design." [Disclaimer statement actually read to students, first on 2005-01-18:] "The state standards require students to learn about Darwin's Theory of Evolution and to eventually take a standardized test of which evolution is a part. Because Darwin's Theory is a theory, it is still being tested as new evidence is discovered. The Theory is not a fact. Gaps in the Theory exist for which there is no evidence. A theory is defined as a well-tested explanation that unifies a broad range of observations. Intelligent Design is an explanation of the origin of life that differs from Darwin's view. The reference book, Of Pandas and People, is available for students to see if they would like to explore this view in an effort to gain an understanding of what Intelligent Design actually involves. As is true with any theory, students are encouraged to keep an open mind. The school leaves the discussion of the Origins of Life up to individual students and their families. As a standards-driven district, class instruction focuses on the standards and preparing students to be successful on standards-based assessments."
content.sourceDocument: Dover Area School Board meeting minutes / Kitzmiller v. Dover trial exhibit

content.label: Pennsylvania 2002 standard 3.3.10.D: analyze the theory of evolution
content.issuingBody: Pennsylvania State Board of Education
content.statementText: [Standard 3.3.10.D, as finally adopted, within 3.3 Biological Sciences, subsection D. Evolution:] students must "analyze the theory of evolution." pennsylvania-lpm.title: Pennsylvania 2022 STEELS standards, Discipline 3.1 Life Science: evolution/natural-selection benchmarks

content.label: Pennsylvania 2022 STEELS standards, Discipline 3.1 Life Science: evolution/natural-selection benchmarks
content.issuingBody: Pennsylvania State Board of Education
content.statementText: [Discipline 3.1 Life Science, Strand "Evidence of Common Ancestry and Diversity," benchmark 3.1.9-12.S:] "Communicate scientific information that common ancestry and biological evolution are supported by multiple lines of empirical evidence." [Strand "Natural Selection," benchmark 3.1.9-12.T:] "Construct an explanation based on evidence that the process of evolution primarily results from four factors: (1) the potential for a species to increase in number, (2) the heritable genetic variation of individuals in a species due to mutation and sexual reproduction, (3) competition for limited resources, and (4) the proliferation of those organisms that are better able to survive and reproduce in the environment." [Strand "Adaptation," benchmark 3.1.9-12.W:] "Construct an explanation based on evidence for how natural selection leads to adaptation of populations." [The full benchmark set -- 3.1.9-12.P through X at high school, 3.1.6-8.M through T at middle school, covering inheritance of traits, variation of traits, evidence of common ancestry, natural selection, and adaptation -- is reproduced in full in case/pennsylvania-steels-2022-evolution-benchmarks.json.]

content.label: All 8 Dover biology teachers refuse to read the disclaimer; it is read by administrators instead

content.label: Kitzmiller v. Dover trial held before Judge John E. Jones III
content.description: Six weeks of testimony in Harrisburg, PA, before Judge John E. Jones III (US District Court, Middle District of Pennsylvania; a George W. Bush appointee). Plaintiffs' expert witnesses included Kenneth R. Miller (Brown University), Barbara Forrest (SE Louisiana University -- testified on the "cdesign proponentsists" find-and-replace artifact in draft manuscripts of "Of Pandas and People"), Kevin Padian, Robert Pennock, John Haught, Brian Alters. Defense expert witnesses Michael Behe (Lehigh University) and Scott Minnich (University of Idaho) testified on "irreducible complexity" (the bacterial flagellum argument); three other Discovery-Institute-affiliated experts (William Dembski, Stephen Meyer, John Angus Campbell) had withdrawn before depositions.

Ousted incumbents included board president Sheila Harkins and former board president Alan Bonsell. The new board's stated position was that it would drop the policy regardless of the pending court ruling.
