pennsylvania-lpm.title: Judge Jones rules the intelligent-design policy unconstitutional

content.label: Judge Jones rules the intelligent-design policy unconstitutional
content.description: Judge John E. Jones III issued a 139-page opinion, Kitzmiller v. Dover Area School District, 400 F. Supp. 2d 707 (M.D. Pa. 2005). Found intelligent design is not science (it invokes a supernatural designer, "a hallmark of a religious, rather than scientific, position") and is a form of creationism relabeled (citing the "cdesign proponentsists" evidence); applied both the Lemon v. Kurtzman test and the endorsement test to find the board acted with religious intent, violating the Establishment Clause. Wrote: "The breathtaking inanity of the Board's decision is evident when considered against the factual backdrop which has now been fully revealed through this trial." Found board members Buckingham and Bonsell gave false testimony denying the policy's religious origins. Not appealed.

pennsylvania-lpm.title: Pennsylvania HB 1007 (2005) would have authorized intelligent-design teaching statewide; dies in committee

content.label: Pennsylvania HB 1007 (2005) would have authorized intelligent-design teaching statewide; dies in committee
content.description: House Bill 1007 would have let local school boards add "intelligent design" to any curriculum that included evolution and let teachers introduce "supporting evidence" for ID. Got a hearing in the House Subcommittee on Basic Education in June 2005, while the Dover trial was underway, but never advanced further -- died in committee. No PA state "academic freedom act" targeting K-12 evolution instruction has ever passed, before or after Dover.

tennessee-lpm.title: American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU)

content.label: American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU)
content.role: National civil-liberties organization. Placed the 1925 newspaper advertisement (reported May 4, 1925) offering to defend any Tennessee teacher willing to test the Butler Act -- the advertisement George Rappleyea and Dayton's civic boosters answered by recruiting John Scopes, making the ACLU the direct originator of the Scopes Trial as a deliberately engineered test case. Its attorney Arthur Garfield Hays joined Scopes's defense team. Forty-two years later, the ACLU (via attorney William Kunstler) also represented Gary Scott, the teacher whose 1967 firing triggered the Butler Act's repeal -- a genuinely different kind of case (a real firing, not a staged test).

tennessee-lpm.title: When a recurring legislative fight loses in court, the next round tends to arrive in secularized language, not a changed goal

content.label: When a recurring legislative fight loses in court, the next round tends to arrive in secularized language, not a changed goal
content.statement: Tennessee's own hundred-year record shows the same underlying question -- should a biblical account of human origins get special legal protection in the science classroom -- pursued through three legislatively distinct mechanisms, each one measurably more secular-sounding than the last: an outright criminal prohibition (1925), a mandate to teach Genesis with "equal emphasis" (1973, struck down specifically for naming the Bible), and a law protecting "scientific strengths and weaknesses" that never names religion at all (2012, still standing). A curriculum-policy archive that only reads each era's law on its own terms, without comparing it to what came before, would miss that the softening itself is the pattern -- and would risk taking 2012's secular framing at face value rather than reading it as a direct, legible response to why 1973 lost in court.
content.rationale: This is an inference this repo's own research drew from comparing three real statutes' text side by side (see TNLP-FINDING-1973-law-vs-2012-law-framing-shift) -- not a claim any named 2012 legislator stated outright the way Rep. Bill Carter explicitly did for the 1973 bill. The principle is offered as a documented pattern worth watching for in any other jurisdiction's own recurring legislative fight, not as a settled fact about anyone's stated intent in 2012.

tennessee-lpm.title: A law nobody has prosecuted under, or ever invoked, is still a real curriculum mandate worth documenting precisely

content.label: A law nobody has prosecuted under, or ever invoked, is still a real curriculum mandate worth documenting precisely
content.statement: The Butler Act itself was enforced exactly once (Scopes) in its 42-year life, by its own governor's admission expected never to be used at all. The 2012 Teacher Protection Act, per this repo's own research, has apparently never been invoked in a documented case either. Neither fact makes either law less real as a legal requirement teachers and districts must account for -- a curriculum- policy archive's job is to document what a jurisdiction's law actually says and requires, independent of how often, or whether, it has ever been tested in practice.
content.rationale: Worth stating explicitly because it would be easy to under-document a law that "doesn't seem to matter" in daily practice. Tennessee's own history argues the opposite: an unenforced law can still produce a landmark national trial decades after its passage (nobody enforcing the Butler Act in 1925 predicted Scopes), and a currently-untested law can still be cited by this exact kind of archive as live, binding, and worth tracking for exactly that reason.

tennessee-lpm.title: The Scopes Trial is a real, concrete case study in how scientific consensus and public institutions actually interact under pressure

content.label: The Scopes Trial is a real, concrete case study in how scientific consensus and public institutions actually interact under pressure
content.statement: A hundred years on, Tennessee's own Scopes Trial -- an engineered test case, a media circus, a courtroom cross-examination of a public figure's own literalist beliefs, and a conviction reversed on a technicality rather than a verdict on the science -- is exactly the kind of worked example OpenEvo's Nature of Science and civic-reasoning goals can draw on directly: how a legal system, a press corps, and a scientific community actually responded to a real controversy, not a hypothetical one. The repeated recurrence of the same underlying question in 1973 and 2012 extends the lesson: this is not a closed, one-time historical event but a documented, recurring pattern a student can trace across a full century using this repo's own recurrenceOf chain.
content.rationale: Same underlying payoff florida-lpm's own equivalent principle names: once a controversy is modeled as a structured record rather than left as prose, it becomes something a curriculum designer can build a lesson or unit from directly. Tennessee's century-long chain is the single richest version of this payoff in this ecosystem so far.

tennessee-lpm.title: From outright prohibition (1925) to mandated alternative-teaching (1973) -- a real shift in legislative strategy

content.label: From outright prohibition (1925) to mandated alternative-teaching (1973) -- a real shift in legislative strategy

commensurate attention to, and an equal amount of emphasis on... the Genesis account in the Bible
objects.sourceDocument: Chapter 377 of the 1973 Public Acts of Tennessee

content.summary: The 1925 Butler Act banned teaching evolution outright. The 1973 law took a structurally different approach: it did not ban evolution, but required Genesis be taught alongside it with "equal emphasis," and required evolution carry a disclaimer that the Bible did not. Forty-eight years apart, the same underlying goal (protect a biblical account of human origins from being taught as settled over evolution) was pursued through a legislatively different mechanism -- a prohibition replaced by a mandated-alternative-plus-disclaimer approach.

tennessee-lpm.title: From explicit religious framing (1973) to secular "critical thinking" framing (2012) -- language softened, underlying goal arguably continuous

content.label: From explicit religious framing (1973) to secular "critical thinking" framing (2012) -- language softened, underlying goal arguably continuous

objects.excerptText: the Genesis account in the Bible
objects.sourceDocument: Chapter 377 of the 1973 Public Acts of Tennessee

objects.excerptText: scientific strengths and scientific weaknesses of existing scientific theories

content.summary: Where the 1973 law named the Bible and Genesis explicitly, the 2012 law uses entirely secular-sounding language ("scientific strengths and weaknesses," "critical thinking") and never mentions religion, creationism, or intelligent design by name. Rep. Bill Carter's own 1973 framing ("duty bound... since I unsuccessfully opposed the repeal") shows explicit continuity of intent between the 1925 and 1973 episodes; no comparably explicit statement of continuity between 1973 and 2012 was found in this repo's research, but Tennessee's 2012 law is textually and functionally the same template Louisiana enacted in 2008 (the "second state" framing, per NCSE) -- a template designed, nationally, after Kitzmiller v. Dover (2005, see pennsylvania-lpm) specifically to avoid the religious language a court could rule unconstitutional.
content.policyRelevance: Evidence for why TNLP-CONTROVERSY-tn-2012-teacher-protection-act has never been challenged in court the way the 1973 law was: its careful avoidance of explicit religious language is plausibly a direct, strategic response to Daniel v. Waters' own reasoning (the 1973 law was struck down specifically for its special treatment of "the Genesis account"), not an indication the underlying political goal changed.
content.exhaustivenessCaveat: The claim that 2012's secular framing is a deliberate response to Daniel v. Waters' specific legal reasoning is this repo's own interpretive inference, grounded in the two rulings/statutes' own text, not a sourced quotation from a 2012 legislator making that connection explicitly -- flagged as inference, not direct testimony, unlike Rep. Carter's own explicit 1973 continuity statement.

tennessee-lpm.title: The Butler Act and the Scopes "Monkey Trial" (1925-1927)

content.label: The Butler Act and the Scopes "Monkey Trial" (1925-1927)
content.topicArea: Whether Tennessee may criminally prohibit public-school teachers from teaching evolution in favor of the biblical account of human origins.
content.summary: Tennessee's 1925 Butler Act made teaching evolution a crime. The ACLU deliberately engineered a test prosecution in Dayton, recruiting teacher John Scopes; the resulting trial pitted Clarence Darrow against William Jennings Bryan in a national media spectacle. Scopes was convicted and fined, but the Tennessee Supreme Court reversed the conviction on a sentencing technicality in 1927 while explicitly upholding the law's constitutionality and urging the state not to pursue the matter further -- ending enforcement without the law ever being struck down.
content.outcomeSummary: Neither side got a clean, lasting win: the ACLU failed to get the Butler Act declared unconstitutional (the Tennessee Supreme Court upheld it), while the state lost its only conviction under the law and the Court itself signaled the prosecution should not continue. The law remained on the books, unenforced in any further prosecution, until its 1967 repeal.

contestedObjects.description: Whether the Butler Act's criminal prohibition on teaching evolution is constitutional, and whether John Scopes's specific conviction under it should stand.

positions.stanceSummary: Engineered the test case specifically to challenge the Butler Act's constitutionality, providing Scopes's defense team.

Joined the prosecution to defend the Butler Act and biblical literalism; his own testimony under Darrow's cross-examination ("I'll leave the agnostics to hunt for her" wife of Cain) was widely seen as damaging to his position.
Lead defense attorney; called Bryan himself as a witness to directly challenge biblical literalism in open court.

positions.actorLabel: Tennessee Supreme Court (Chief Justice Grafton Green)
positions.stanceSummary: Upheld the Butler Act's constitutionality but reversed Scopes's conviction on a sentencing technicality, writing "nothing is to be gained by prolonging the life of this bizarre case" and recommending the state not retry Scopes.

tennessee-lpm.title: The 1973 "equal time" / "Genesis Bill" and its 1975 invalidation

content.label: The 1973 "equal time" / "Genesis Bill" and its 1975 invalidation
content.topicArea: Whether Tennessee may require biology textbooks give the Genesis account "equal emphasis" with evolution and label evolution "not... scientific fact."
content.summary: Six years after repealing the Butler Act, Tennessee passed a new law -- championed explicitly as continuing the earlier fight by a legislator representing Dayton's own county -- requiring textbooks teach the Genesis account alongside evolution with equal weight. Tennessee biology teachers, parents, and the National Association of Biology Teachers sued; the Sixth Circuit struck the law down as patently unconstitutional in 1975, less than two years after it passed.
content.outcomeSummary: The law was struck down in full by the Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals, which called it "patently unconstitutional" on two independent grounds. Not appealed further -- a clean, substantive defeat for the side that wanted the change, unlike the 1925 episode's technicality- based non-resolution.

contestedObjects.description: Whether Tennessee law may require Genesis be taught alongside evolution with "equal emphasis" and require evolution (but not the Bible) carry a disclaimer that it is "not... scientific fact."

positions.stanceSummary: Championed the bill explicitly as continuing the earlier Scopes-era fight: "Since I unsuccessfully opposed the repeal of the 'Evolution Law'... I have been duty bound to do all I can to see that this bill is passed."

positions.stanceSummary: Sued the state textbook board, arguing the law unconstitutionally preferred the biblical account of creation.

tennessee-lpm.title: The 2012 Tennessee Teacher Protection Act ("monkey law")

content.label: The 2012 Tennessee Teacher Protection Act ("monkey law")
content.topicArea: Whether Tennessee teachers should be explicitly protected from discipline for presenting "scientific weaknesses" of evolution, climate change, and other named theories.
content.summary: Nearly 40 years after Daniel v. Waters struck down Tennessee's religiously-framed 1973 law, the legislature passed a new law using entirely secular language -- "scientific strengths and weaknesses," never naming religion, creationism, or intelligent design directly. Governor Haslam let it become law without his signature, calling it unclear rather than objectionable. It passed over organized opposition from national and Tennessee-specific science-education bodies, and remains in force today, apparently never challenged in court.
content.outcomeSummary: The law took effect and remains in force as of this repo's founding session (2026), the only one of Tennessee's three central statutes never invalidated, repealed, or amended -- though also, per this session's research, apparently never tested in court or shown to have been actually invoked by any teacher or district.

contestedObjects.description: Whether Tennessee teachers should be explicitly shielded from discipline for presenting "scientific strengths and weaknesses" of evolution and other named theories.

positions.actorLabel: Sen. Bo Watson and Rep. Bill Dunn (sponsors)
positions.stanceSummary: Framed the bill as promoting critical thinking and objective scientific inquiry, not an attack on evolution specifically.

Let the bill become law without his signature rather than veto or sign it: "good legislation should bring clarity and not confusion. My concern is that this bill has not met this objective" -- a deliberately ambivalent position, neither endorsing nor blocking it.

positions.actorLabel: National Center for Science Education (Eugenie C. Scott)
positions.stanceSummary: "Telling students that evolution and climate change are scientifically controversial is miseducating them."
Called the bill "unnecessary, anti-scientific, and very likely unconstitutional," warning it would let teachers "teach a Sunday school class" in science class.

content.statementText: Chapter 377 of the 1973 Public Acts of Tennessee: required that any biology textbook expressing an opinion on "origins or creation of man and his world" give "commensurate attention to, and an equal amount of emphasis on" other theories, "including, but not limited to, the Genesis account in the Bible," and required textbooks discussing evolution state it was "not represented to be scientific fact" -- a disclaimer not applied to the Bible, which the statute itself defined as a "reference work."

content.label: The Tennessee Teacher Protection Act (2012, "monkey law")
content.issuingBody: Tennessee General Assembly / allowed to become law without Governor Bill Haslam's signature
content.statementText: T.C.A. tennessee-lpm.title: Rep. John Washington Butler introduces House Bill No. 185

content.label: Rep. John Washington Butler introduces House Bill No. 185
content.description: Rep. John Washington Butler introduced House Bill No. 185, making it unlawful for any teacher in a state-funded Tennessee school or university to teach "any theory that denies the story of the Divine Creation of man as taught in the Bible" in favor of descent "from a lower order of animals," with a misdemeanor penalty of $100-$500 per offense.

provenance.sourceProvenance: Wikipedia, "Butler Act," cross-checked against the full statutory text hosted at todayinsci.com.

tennessee-lpm.title: Governor Austin Peay signs the Butler Act into law

content.label: Governor Austin Peay signs the Butler Act into law
content.description: Following House passage 71-5 (Jan 28) and Senate passage 24-6 (Mar 13), Governor Austin Peay signed the Butler Act. Peay said "nothing of consequence in the books now being taught in our schools" would run afoul of it, that "the people must have the right to regulate what is taught in their schools," and that he did not believe it would ever actually be enforced.

provenance.sourceProvenance: Wikipedia, "Austin Peay," fetched and read directly.

tennessee-lpm.title: ACLU advertises for a test-case teacher; Dayton boosters recruit John Scopes

content.label: ACLU advertises for a test-case teacher; Dayton boosters recruit John Scopes
content.description: The ACLU's newspaper advertisement (reported in the Chattanooga Times) offered to defend any Tennessee teacher willing to test the Butler Act. George Rappleyea, a Dayton engineer and civic booster, convinced a group of Dayton businessmen at Robinson's Drug Store to recruit John T. Scopes, a local substitute teacher/football coach, as the test defendant -- explicitly to generate publicity and business for the town.

provenance.sourceProvenance: Wikipedia, "George Rappleyea"; Science History Institute, "The Scopes Monkey Trial Publicity Stunt" -- both fetched and read directly.

tennessee-lpm.title: The Scopes Trial -- Darrow, Bryan, and a guilty verdict

content.label: The Scopes Trial -- Darrow, Bryan, and a guilty verdict
content.description: Rhea County Courthouse, Dayton, Tennessee. Judge John T. Raulston. Prosecution: District Attorney Tom Stewart, Herbert E. Hicks, Sue K. Hicks, Gordon McKenzie, joined by William Jennings Bryan. Defense: Clarence Darrow (lead), Arthur Garfield Hays (ACLU), Dudley Field Malone, John R. Neal, W.O. Thompson, F.B. McElwee. On day 7, with the jury excused, Darrow called Bryan to the stand to question his literal reading of the Bible -- asked where Cain found his wife, Bryan replied he'd "leave the agnostics to hunt for her," an exchange generally treated as having damaged Bryan's credibility even though Raulston struck the testimony the next day. Scopes was found guilty and fined $100 (set by the judge, not the jury -- the basis of the 1927 reversal). H.L. Mencken's Baltimore Sun coverage coined "Monkey Trial"; this was the first American trial broadcast live nationally by radio (Chicago's WGN).

provenance.sourceProvenance: Wikipedia, "Scopes trial"; Science History Institute -- both fetched and read directly.

tennessee-lpm.title: William Jennings Bryan dies in Dayton, five days after the trial

content.label: William Jennings Bryan dies in Dayton, five days after the trial
content.description: Bryan died in his sleep (reported stroke) in Dayton, Tennessee, after church and an afternoon nap. H.L. Mencken privately remarked "We killed the son-of-a-bitch!" and his published obituary (Baltimore Evening Sun, July 27) was openly hostile, calling Bryan "a vulgar and common man."

provenance.sourceProvenance: Wikipedia, "William Jennings Bryan"; NCSE, "Stop Press! Mencken's Obituary for Bryan" -- both fetched and read directly.

tennessee-lpm.title: Tennessee Supreme Court upholds the Butler Act but reverses Scopes's conviction on a technicality

content.label: Tennessee Supreme Court upholds the Butler Act but reverses Scopes's conviction on a technicality
content.description: Scopes v. State, 289 S.W. 363, 154 Tenn. 105 (Tenn. 1927). A 3-1 decision, Chief Justice Grafton Green writing: the Butler Act was held constitutional, but Scopes's conviction was reversed because Tennessee law required fines over $50 be set by a jury, not a judge -- the judge-imposed $100 fine was improper. The court wrote "nothing is to be gained by prolonging the life of this bizarre case" and recommended the state enter a nolle prosequi rather than retry Scopes, "to preserve the peace and dignity of the state" -- deliberately ending the prosecution without striking the law itself. The state did not retry Scopes.
content.licenseOrRightsNote: A state appellate court's own published opinion is a public judicial record.

provenance.contributor_notes: Exact day of the ruling is disputed across secondary sources (January 14 vs. 17, 1927) -- dateStart recorded at month granularity pending confirmation of the exact day against a primary court record.
provenance.sourceProvenance: TIME archive, "Education: Bizarre"; Americans United, "Scopes forever" -- both fetched and read directly.

tennessee-lpm.license_or_rights_note: A state appellate court's own published opinion is a public judicial record.

tennessee-lpm.title: Gary Scott fired for teaching evolution, triggering the Butler Act's repeal

content.label: Gary Scott fired for teaching evolution, triggering the Butler Act's repeal
content.description: Gary L. Scott, a science teacher in Jacksboro, Tennessee, was fired for teaching evolution -- unlike Scopes, not a staged test case; Scott said he didn't realize he'd broken the law. He sued for reinstatement on First Amendment grounds, represented by William Kunstler (later the Chicago Seven's attorney) with ACLU support.

provenance.sourceProvenance: Knox TN Today, "His name was Gary Scott, and he is a hero," fetched and read directly.

tennessee-lpm.title: Tennessee repeals the Butler Act within days of Scott's lawsuit

content.label: Tennessee repeals the Butler Act within days of Scott's lawsuit
content.description: Within three days of Gary Scott's lawsuit being filed, a repeal bill (House Bill No. 48, Chapter No. 237) passed both chambers of the Tennessee legislature on May 13, 1967. Governor Buford Ellington signed it (exact day disputed between May 17 and 18 across sources). Effective September 1, 1967 -- roughly 18 months before the US Supreme Court's Epperson v. Arkansas (decided Nov 12, 1968) struck down a near-identical Arkansas law; Tennessee's repeal was driven independently by the Scott controversy, not a response to Epperson.

provenance.contributor_notes: Exact signing day (May 17 vs. 18, 1967) disputed across secondary sources; May 18 is better supported.
provenance.sourceProvenance: Wikipedia, "Butler Act"; Scientific American, "50 Years Ago: Repeal of Tennessee's Monkey Law" -- both fetched and read directly.

tennessee-lpm.title: US Supreme Court strikes down Arkansas's near-identical anti-evolution law

content.label: US Supreme Court strikes down Arkansas's near-identical anti-evolution law
content.description: Epperson v. Arkansas, 393 U.S. 97 (1968) -- not a Tennessee case, but directly relevant context: the US Supreme Court struck down Arkansas's own Butler-Act-style anti-evolution law as an unconstitutional establishment of religion. Tennessee had already repealed its own Butler Act roughly 18 months earlier, independently of this ruling (see TNLP-EVENT-butler-act-repealed) -- included here to make that timing relationship explicit and checkable rather than assumed.
content.licenseOrRightsNote: A US Supreme Court ruling is a public judicial record.

provenance.contributor_notes: This record exists to document the TIMING relationship with Tennessee's own 1967 repeal, not as a primary finding about Arkansas law -- the case itself was not independently re-verified beyond what the Butler Act research already corroborated.
provenance.sourceProvenance: Referenced via Wikipedia's "Butler Act" article and Scientific American's retrospective, both fetched directly in service of the Tennessee repeal research.

tennessee-lpm.title: Dr. Russell Artist begins pushing for an "equal time" law

content.label: Dr. Russell Artist begins pushing for an "equal time" law
content.description: Dr. Russell Artist, a biology professor at David Lipscomb College, pushed the idea of requiring the Genesis account be taught alongside evolution through the late 1960s/early 1970s, approaching fellow Church of Christ member Sen. Milton H. Hamilton (Union City) to sponsor it.

provenance.sourceProvenance: Journal of Southern Religion, "'Equal Space With Adam and Eve': Tennessee's 'Genesis Bill' of 1973," fetched and read directly.

tennessee-lpm.title: Tennessee passes the 1973 "equal time" / "Genesis Bill"

content.label: Tennessee passes the 1973 "equal time" / "Genesis Bill"
content.description: Senate Bill 394 / House Bill 597, enacted as Chapter 377 of the 1973 Public Acts. Sponsored by Sen. Milton H. Hamilton with House backing from Speaker Ned McWherter and Rep. Tommy Bennett; championed by Rep. Bill Carter of Rhea County (home of the original Scopes trial), who said: "Since I unsuccessfully opposed the repeal of the 'Evolution Law'... I have been duty bound to do all I can to see that this bill is passed." Required biology textbooks discussing "origins or creation of man" to give "commensurate attention to, and an equal amount of emphasis on" other theories "including, but not limited to, the Genesis account in the Bible," and required evolution be presented as "not represented to be scientific fact" -- a disclaimer not applied to the Bible, which the statute defined as a "reference work." Signed by Governor Winfield Dunn.

provenance.sourceProvenance: Journal of Southern Religion, "'Equal Space With Adam and Eve': Tennessee's 'Genesis Bill' of 1973," fetched and read directly.

tennessee-lpm.title: Daniel v. Waters -- federal courts strike down the 1973 law

content.label: Daniel v. Waters -- federal courts strike down the 1973 law
content.description: Tennessee biology teachers and parents, joined by the National Association of Biology Teachers, sued the state textbook board. The federal district court (M.D. Tenn.) initially abstained on the merits (Feb 26, 1974); on remand it found the law gave "a clearly defined preferential position for the Biblical version of creation" (399 F. Supp. 510). The Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals affirmed, 515 F.2d 485 (6th Cir. 1975), decided April 10, 1975 -- Judge George Edwards wrote the majority opinion calling the law "patently unconstitutional" on two grounds: its special treatment of "occult or satanical beliefs," and its special treatment of the Genesis account specifically. Not appealed further.
content.licenseOrRightsNote: Federal court opinions are public judicial records.

provenance.sourceProvenance: Wikipedia, "Daniel v. Waters"; TalkOrigins case summary -- both fetched and read directly.

tennessee-lpm.title: Tennessee Court of Appeals rules LexisNexis is not a state actor

content.label: Tennessee Court of Appeals rules LexisNexis is not a state actor
content.description: Public.Resource.Org v. Matthew Bender & Company, M2022-01260-COA-R3-CV. The Tennessee Court of Appeals ruled LexisNexis is a private contractor, not a state actor, and is not bound by Tennessee's public-records law on this basis -- affirming (with modification) that the Tennessee Code Annotated is exempt from disclosure since state law provides a separate dedicated channel for publishing it (the LexisNexis contract itself). Net effect: Tennessee does not formally claim copyright over its own statutory text, but the complete official annotated code remains gated behind a commercial product, with the courts upholding that arrangement.

us-evolution-education-lpm.title: Florida, Pennsylvania, and Tennessee have three genuinely different current postures on evolution-education policy

content.label: Florida, Pennsylvania, and Tennessee have three genuinely different current postures on evolution-education policy

objects.sourceDocument: Science, Technology & Engineering and Environmental Literacy & Sustainability Standards (STEELS)

content.summary: As of this research (2026-10-20): Florida's CURRENT standards-revision process is actively removing explicit naming of evolution and climate change -- the single most acute live controversy of the three. Pennsylvania's current standards were never themselves a site of evolution controversy (the fight there was Dover's 2004 DISTRICT policy, resolved by litigation in 2005, with the state's own standards never substantively challenged). Tennessee's current 2022 standards are robust on evolution (NCSE graded the prior generation "A" for evolution content specifically) -- but Tennessee is also the only one of the three with an unresolved, currently-active STATUTE (the 2012 Teacher Protection Act) sitting alongside those otherwise strong standards, never challenged in court.
content.policyRelevance: This is the comparison none of the three state repos' own self-contained files can make about themselves -- each is accurate and complete about its own jurisdiction, but only reading all three side by side shows that "a US state's current posture on evolution education" is not one thing: a state can be actively regressing (FL), quiet because its one real fight happened at a different governmental level (PA), or quiet on standards while still carrying a live, untested statute that could resurface (TN).
content.exhaustivenessCaveat: Built from this session's own three state-repo founding research passes, not a fourth, independent cross-state research effort -- accurate as of each repo's own founding date (2026-10-20) and subject to the same caveats as each repo's own records (e.g. no NCSE evaluation of Pennsylvania's or Tennessee's CURRENT standards was found; only older-generation grades exist for comparison).

provenance.sourceProvenance: Synthesized directly from florida-lpm's, pennsylvania-lpm's, and tennessee-lpm's own founding-session records, all built the same day from primary sources -- see each repo's own docs/source-notes/.

us-evolution-education-lpm.title: Tennessee's 2012 law's secular language is legible as a direct response to Edwards v. Aguillard's own reasoning

content.label: Tennessee's 2012 law's secular language is legible as a direct response to Edwards v. Aguillard's own reasoning

objects.excerptText: it is required that the statement of such purpose be sincere and not a sham
scientific strengths and scientific weaknesses of existing scientific theories

content.summary: Edwards struck down Louisiana's 1981 law specifically because its stated "academic freedom" purpose was found insincere -- a pretext for a religious goal, given the law explicitly named "creation science" and the Genesis account. Tennessee's own 1973 law (named explicitly in tennessee-lpm) was struck down on parallel reasoning in 1975 for the same explicit naming. Tennessee's 2012 law never names religion, creationism, or intelligent design at all -- using only "scientific strengths and weaknesses," a framing that, if genuinely secular, would satisfy Edwards' own sincerity requirement.
content.policyRelevance: This finding does not claim to know the 2012 Tennessee legislature's actual subjective intent (no named 2012 legislator was found making this connection explicitly, per tennessee-lpm's own research) -- it states only that the law's text is legally well-designed to survive exactly the test Edwards established, whatever the drafters' own motives actually were.
content.exhaustivenessCaveat: An inference grounded in the two statutes' and the ruling's own text, not a sourced quotation from a 2012 legislator stating this connection outright -- tennessee-lpm's own equivalent finding (TNLP-FINDING-1973-law-vs-2012-law-framing-shift) makes the identical caveat for the same reason.

provenance.sourceProvenance: Edwards v. Aguillard opinion (Cornell LII/FindLaw) and Tennessee Code Annotated S49-6-1030 (Justia) -- both fetched and read directly.

content.label: The American evolution-education culture war, 1925-present
content.topicArea: Whether American public schools may, or must, teach evolution as settled science, unqualified, contested, or legally discouraged -- a single recurring national question fought separately in at least three states' own legislatures, school boards, and courts across a full century.
content.summary: Beginning with Tennessee's 1925 Butler Act and the Scopes Trial, the same underlying question -- should a biblical or religiously-adjacent account of human origins get special legal protection against evolution in the science classroom -- has recurred in different US states, different decades, and different legal mechanisms: Arkansas and Mississippi's own Butler-Act-style bans (struck down by the US Supreme Court and the Mississippi Supreme Court, 1968 and 1970), a 1973 Tennessee "equal time" law (struck down 1975), Louisiana's 1981 "balanced treatment" law (struck down by the US Supreme Court, 1987), a single Pennsylvania school district's 2004 intelligent-design disclaimer (struck down by a federal court, 2005), a wave of "academic freedom act" laws modeled on Discovery Institute's template and designed to survive the 1987 ruling (Louisiana 2008, Tennessee 2012, the latter still in force), and Florida's own recurring state-standards fights (2008, and an active 2026 rewrite). This record does not replace or duplicate florida-lpm's, pennsylvania-lpm's, or tennessee-lpm's own controversy records -- it names the pattern they are each a real, independently-adjudicated instance of.
content.outcomeSummary: No single outcome -- by design, since this is not one dispute but a named pattern across several. Of the specific episodes this record synthesizes: two US Supreme Court rulings (Epperson 1968, Edwards 1987) permanently foreclosed outright bans and explicit "creation-science" mandates nationwide; Pennsylvania's Dover case (2005) and Tennessee's own 1973 law (1975) were struck down at the district/circuit level; Tennessee's 2012 law remains in force, untested; and Florida's 2026 fight is still actively unresolved as of this record's own date.

contestedObjects.description: Whether a state or district may legally discourage, qualify, or omit the teaching of evolution, or mandate a religiously-adjacent alternative be taught alongside it -- the single question underlying every episode this record synthesizes.

positions.stanceSummary: The single most consistent institutional opponent of every restrictive episode this record synthesizes, across its entire multi-decade existence (founded 1981/1983, directly in response to this same wave of state legislative activity).

Authored the "Academic Freedom Act" legislative template directly responsible for the post-Edwards wave (Louisiana 2008, Tennessee 2012), its own 1998 "Wedge Document" strategy memo stating the actual long-term goal was to "replace materialistic explanations with the theistic understanding that nature and human beings are created by God."

A direct participant in multiple episodes across the full century: recruited John Scopes in 1925, filed an amicus brief in Epperson (1968), represented Gary Scott in Tennessee (1967), and was co-counsel for the Kitzmiller plaintiffs in Pennsylvania (2005).

content.exhaustivenessCaveat: Synthesizes only the episodes documented in florida-lpm/pennsylvania-lpm/ tennessee-lpm plus the two national Supreme Court rulings this repo's own research covered directly -- NOT a claim this is the complete universe of US evolution-education controversies (other states -- e.g. Kansas, Texas, Ohio -- have their own real, undocumented-in-this-ecosystem episodes; this record is honest about covering what this ecosystem has actually built so far, not the full national history).

provenance.sourceProvenance: Synthesized from this repo's own national-level research (the two Supreme Court opinions, read directly) plus florida-lpm's/ pennsylvania-lpm's/tennessee-lpm's own founding-session records.

content.label: National Center for Science Education (NCSE)
content.role: Founded by Stanley L. Weinberg, a retired Iowa high school biology teacher, who began organizing state-level "Committees of Correspondence" to track and counter creationist legislative efforts starting in 1980, linked by a Creation/Evolution Newsletter; formally incorporated as NCSE in 1983 (1981 is also commonly cited as the founding/organizing year). The single most consistent institutional voice defending evolution/climate-science education in US public schools for over four decades, with a confirmed, independent role in all three state repos this ecosystem has built so far.

currentHolder.title: Deputy Director

provenance.sourceProvenance: NCSE's own site and Wikipedia's NCSE entry, cross-checked -- fetched and read directly this session.

content.label: American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU)
content.role: Founded 1920 in New York (Roger Baldwin among the founders), emerging from the National Civil Liberties Bureau in response to the WWI-era Palmer Raids -- unrelated to evolution at founding. The Scopes Trial (1925) was one of its earliest and most famous cases: it recruited John Scopes to challenge Tennessee's Butler Act and partnered with Clarence Darrow for his defense. Filed an amicus brief (not direct counsel) supporting Susan Epperson in Epperson v. Arkansas (1968, Leo Pfeffer, Melvin L. Wulf, Joseph B. Robison). Its Pennsylvania affiliate was co-counsel for the Kitzmiller plaintiffs (2005); it also represented Gary Scott in Tennessee (1967).

provenance.sourceProvenance: The Epperson v. Arkansas opinion itself (Library of Congress digitized US Reports volume), read directly; ACLU's own history page (aclu.org/about/aclu-history), fetched and read directly.

us-evolution-education-lpm.title: Discovery Institute (Center for Science and Culture)

content.label: Discovery Institute (Center for Science and Culture)
content.role: Founded 1991 (not 1990, an earlier assumption corrected this session) by Bruce Chapman (a former Reagan-era official) and George Gilder, in Seattle, as a spinoff of the Hudson Institute. Its Center for Science and Culture (originally "Center for the Renewal of Science and Culture," the intelligent-design-focused unit) was established in 1996. Its internal 1998 strategy memo, the "Wedge Document" (leaked 1999-02-05), states its actual long-term goal in its own words: "To defeat scientific materialism and its destructive moral, cultural and political legacies" and "To replace materialistic explanations with the theistic understanding that nature and human beings are created by God." Authored the model "Academic Freedom Act" legislative template (used in Louisiana 2008 and Tennessee 2012) -- language deliberately designed, per NCSE's own analysis, to avoid the specific religious-purpose reasoning Edwards v. Aguillard (1987) used to strike down Louisiana's earlier, more explicit law.

provenance.contributor_notes: No actor record for Discovery Institute exists in tennessee-lpm -- that repo's own research found no direct institutional tie between the Institute and Tennessee's 2012 law specifically, so no crossRepoRef to tennessee-lpm is added here either (an informal cross-reference should not assert a connection a sibling repo's own research did not confirm).
provenance.sourceProvenance: Discovery Institute's own history page (discovery.org/f/4441/); the Wedge Document itself, hosted in full by NCSE (ncse.ngo/wedge-document) -- both fetched and read directly.

us-evolution-education-lpm.title: Epperson v. Arkansas, 393 U.S. 97 (1968): states may not ban teaching evolution

content.label: Epperson v. Arkansas, 393 U.S. 97 (1968): states may not ban teaching evolution
content.issuingBody: Supreme Court of the United States
content.statementText: "[T]he law must be stricken because of its conflict with the constitutional prohibition of state laws respecting an establishment of religion or prohibiting the free exercise thereof. The overriding fact is that Arkansas' law selects from the body of knowledge a particular segment which it proscribes for the sole reason that it is deemed to conflict with a particular religious doctrine; that is, with a particular interpretation of the Book of Genesis by a particular religious group." "Government in our democracy, state and national, must be neutral in matters of religious theory, doctrine, and practice... The First Amendment mandates governmental neutrality between religion and religion, and between religion and nonreligion."
content.sourceDocument: Epperson v. Arkansas, 393 U.S. 97 (1968)
content.licenseOrRightsNote: A US Supreme Court opinion is a public judicial record, not subject to copyright.

provenance.contributor_notes: Unanimous in result (9-0, Justice Abe Fortas writing for the Court) but not in reasoning -- Black, Harlan, and Stewart each wrote separate concurrences; Black doubted the case was even "genuinely justiciable" since Arkansas had never once enforced the law in 40 years. The Court's own opinion states directly that the Arkansas statute "was an adaptation of the famous Tennessee 'monkey law' which that State adopted in 1925" -- the direct doctrinal lineage from tennessee-lpm's own Butler Act. Footnote 8 confirms Mississippi had an identical law still on the books in 1968 (struck down separately, Smith v. State, 242 So. 2d 692 (Miss. 1970)) and that Tennessee's own law had already been repealed by 1967.
provenance.sourceProvenance: Library of Congress's own digitized US Reports volume, fetched and read directly -- the actual opinion text, not a summary.

us-evolution-education-lpm.title: Edwards v. Aguillard, 482 U.S. 578 (1987): states may not mandate "creation science" alongside evolution

content.label: Edwards v. Aguillard, 482 U.S. 578 (1987): states may not mandate "creation science" alongside evolution
content.issuingBody: Supreme Court of the United States
content.statementText: "While the Court is normally deferential to a State's articulation of a secular purpose, it is required that the statement of such purpose be sincere and not a sham." "The preeminent purpose of the Louisiana Legislature was clearly to advance the religious viewpoint that a supernatural being created humankind." The Act "does not grant teachers a flexibility that they did not already possess" and was "designed either to promote the theory of creation science which embodies a particular religious tenet or to prohibit the teaching of a scientific theory disfavored by certain religious sects."
content.sourceDocument: Edwards v. Aguillard, 482 U.S. 578 (1987)
content.licenseOrRightsNote: A US Supreme Court opinion is a public judicial record, not subject to copyright.

provenance.contributor_notes: 7-2, Justice William Brennan writing for the Court; Justice Scalia dissented, joined by Chief Justice Rehnquist, arguing the majority too readily inferred unconstitutional religious motive from a law stating a facially secular ("academic freedom") purpose. Reached the Supreme Court via summary judgment on the pleadings and legislative history alone -- no trial record, unlike pennsylvania-lpm's Kitzmiller, which was a full six-week trial. This ruling's own reasoning (a law survives only if its secular purpose is sincere, not a sham) is the direct doctrinal target the later "academic freedom act" template (Louisiana 2008, tennessee-lpm's own 2012 law) was designed around -- see this repo's own national_ccs_policy/records/coherence-findings.yaml.
provenance.sourceProvenance: Cornell Legal Information Institute's and FindLaw's hosted opinion text, cross-checked against each other -- both verbatim reproductions, fetched and read directly.

us-evolution-education-lpm.title: A real, documented national pattern is not the same thing as a single national rule, and a curriculum archive should keep the two distinct

content.label: A real, documented national pattern is not the same thing as a single national rule, and a curriculum archive should keep the two distinct
content.statement: Two US Supreme Court rulings genuinely bind every state at once on this question. Everything else this ecosystem has documented -- Florida's recurring state fights, Pennsylvania's district-level litigation, Tennessee's century of statutes -- is a separate, independently-adjudicated dispute in its own jurisdiction, connected to the others only by a real, documented, continuous underlying question, not by a shared legal proceeding or a single governing body. `policy-controversy-record.controversyType: cross-jurisdiction-pattern` exists specifically so a curriculum-policy archive can name that kind of connection honestly, without either ignoring it (treating each state as if it had no relationship to the others) or overstating it (writing as if "the United States" itself were one single disputing party with one single legal outcome, the way a single state's own controversy record legitimately can be written).
content.rationale: This is the single structural lesson of this repo's own founding: the three state repos, each internally accurate and complete, were genuinely missing a layer that is distinct from any one of them -- and building that layer required one new schema value (`cross-jurisdiction-pattern`) and one new field (`crossRepoRefs`), not a restructuring of anything already built.

us-evolution-education-lpm.title: A landmark ruling changes what the next legislative attempt looks like; it rarely ends the underlying attempt

content.label: A landmark ruling changes what the next legislative attempt looks like; it rarely ends the underlying attempt
content.statement: Epperson (1968) ended outright teaching bans. Edwards (1987) ended explicit "creation science" mandates. Neither ruling ended the underlying legislative effort to protect a religiously-motivated alternative to evolution in public education -- each one instead produced a next-generation template, engineered specifically to avoid the exact legal defect the ruling identified, with Tennessee's 2012 law (still standing, untested) as the clearest documented example in this ecosystem so far.
content.rationale: Grounded directly in USLP-FINDING-edwards-reasoning-vs-2012-tennessee-law and tennessee-lpm's own parallel finding -- this is a pattern this ecosystem's own research actually traced across two real rulings and three real statutes, not a general claim about litigation's limits stated in the abstract.

us-evolution-education-lpm.title: Supreme Court strikes down Arkansas's outright evolution-teaching ban

content.label: Supreme Court strikes down Arkansas's outright evolution-teaching ban
content.description: Epperson v. Arkansas, 393 U.S. 97 (1968). Unanimous (9-0), Justice Abe Fortas writing. Struck down Arkansas's Initiated Act No. 1 (1928) -- itself, per the Court's own opinion, "an adaptation of the famous Tennessee 'monkey law' which that State adopted in 1925" -- as an unconstitutional establishment of religion. Tennessee had already repealed its own law roughly 18 months earlier (see tennessee-lpm); Mississippi's identical law was struck down separately two years later (Smith v. State, 1970).

us-evolution-education-lpm.title: Supreme Court strikes down Louisiana's "balanced treatment" creationism law

content.label: Supreme Court strikes down Louisiana's "balanced treatment" creationism law
content.description: Edwards v. Aguillard, 482 U.S. 578 (1987). 7-2, Justice William Brennan writing; Scalia dissented, joined by Rehnquist. Struck down Louisiana's "Balanced Treatment for Creation-Science and Evolution-Science Act" (1981), finding its stated "academic freedom" purpose a sham for a religious one. Reached the Court via summary judgment, not a trial. This ruling's own reasoning is the specific legal target the later "academic freedom act" template (Louisiana 2008, Tennessee 2012 -- see tennessee-lpm) was designed around, avoiding explicit religious language to survive it.

us-evolution-education-lpm.title: Mississippi Supreme Court strikes down its own identical anti-evolution law

content.label: Mississippi Supreme Court strikes down its own identical anti-evolution law
content.description: Smith v. State, 242 So. 2d 692 (Miss. 1970). The Mississippi Supreme Court held Epperson v. Arkansas had "for all practical purposes already held that our anti-evolution statutes are unconstitutional" -- Mississippi and Arkansas were, per Epperson's own footnote 8, the only two states that still had Butler-Act-style teaching bans on the books as of 1968.
